=== PAPER 3a13b1eecbf9 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the core problem as reliably extracting high-quality samples and expectation values from noisy near-term quantum devices, which is a key scaling bottleneck for sample-based algorithms such as variational optimization and machine learning applied to risk and optimization tasks. The authors emphasize that noise on current hardware makes leveraging near-term quantum computers difficult, and they therefore seek to formally quantify the sampling overhead required to obtain ‘good’ samples under a specified noise model.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-007, C-009, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: Methodologically, the work assumes a layered Pauli-Lindblad noise model and leverages a protocol that enables efficient learning of layerwise noise coefficients, summarized by an aggregate noise parameter γ that quantifies overall noise strength. Layer fidelity is used as a practical metric to relate this model to sampling costs, with per-layer fidelities multiplying across layers, and the authors extend their framework to diagonal and non-diagonal Hamiltonians via commuting-Pauli decompositions and to applications such as QAOA, fidelity estimation, and QSVM kernels. They also introduce the use of CVaR on noisy measurement distributions, possibly combined with problem-informed filter functions, to obtain provable bounds on noise-free expectation values and to post-select samples consistent with known problem structure.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main theoretical result is that under the assumed noise model, obtaining a target bitstring from a noisy device requires a multiplicative sampling overhead scaling as √γ, where γ encodes noise strength, and that this scaling carries over to the sampling cost in CVaR-based expectation estimation. A central contribution is the proof that CVaR of noisy samples yields rigorous upper and lower bounds on noise-free expectation values; for diagonal Hamiltonians these bounds apply directly, and in the special case where the ideal state is a ground state, the lower CVaR bound becomes tight and furthermore lower bounds the fidelity between noisy and ideal states at level α when CVaR equals the ground energy. The variance of the CVaR estimator is shown to be bounded as O(1/α²) in general and O(1/α) for Bernoulli and normal-like cases, and the authors show that exploiting problem structure via filtered Hamiltonians and constraint-preserving ansätze can significantly tighten these bounds and ensure that post-selected averages remain within filtered CVaR intervals. They demonstrate that their results directly apply to QAOA and argue that, given a √γ sampling overhead, known QAOA approximation guarantees can be retained in the presence of noise, with experiments up to 40 and 127 qubits confirming the CVaR-bound behavior and revealing that fitted effective γ can be smaller than conservative layer-fidelity estimates. Additional experiments validate the variance-scaling predictions via bootstrapping and show that 40-qubit QAOA MAXCUT CVaR values upper-bound ideal expectations as predicted, while 127-qubit tests highlight that applying the analytic CVaR bounds requires shot counts that are currently impractical.
    [codes: C-001, C-013, C-015, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-004]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors position their CVaR-based bounding approach against classical and quantum baselines by noting that, under the assumed noise model, a √γ sampling overhead can in principle recover known classical QAOA approximation guarantees even in the noisy regime, provided sufficient samples are taken. They explicitly compare their sampling overhead to that of probabilistic error cancellation, stating that their method requires considerably fewer samples—scaling like √γ rather than γ²—but only provides bounds on expectation values rather than unbiased estimators, implying a trade-off between sample efficiency and estimator bias relative to more resource-intensive quantum error mitigation schemes.
    [codes: C-032, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper emphasizes that implementing full quantum error correction on current devices is infeasible, motivating the need for mitigation but also constraining achievable accuracy. The authors acknowledge that their core analysis focuses on gate and circuit noise and largely omits state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors, explicitly noting that SPAM is a separate issue and that their primary focus is on errors during circuit execution. They further recognize that, for some problem sizes and hardware qualities, the √γ sampling overhead required to combat noise may exceed the cost of brute-force classical search, undermining any practical advantage, and they show that for their 127-qubit experiments the number of shots required to apply the analytic CVaR bounds is ‘significantly higher’ and currently impractical to run. They also highlight that hardware quality thresholds and low layer fidelities can lead to enormous required sampling overheads, limiting near-term applicability even if the theoretical bounds hold.
    [codes: C-006, C-016, C-033, C-040, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest exploring hybrid workflows where classical optimization is used to determine variational parameters and quantum hardware is employed only for sampling good solutions, leveraging their sampling and CVaR guarantees in a more hardware-efficient way. They also propose extending their methodology to explicitly account for SPAM errors, indicating that adapting the CVaR-based framework and noise modeling to include SPAM is a natural direction for future research.
    [codes: C-031, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its core contribution a formal quantification of the sampling overhead needed to obtain high-quality samples from noisy quantum computers, expressed in terms of an aggregate noise parameter γ and linked to experimentally accessible layer fidelities. Building on this, the authors introduce the use of CVaR of noisy samples to derive provable bounds on noise-free expectation values, extending these bounds to diagonal and general Hamiltonians, and show how problem-specific filters and constraint-preserving ansätze can tighten the bounds and even infer fidelity guarantees in ground-state settings. They further highlight that their √γ sampling and variance scaling represent a more favorable overhead than probabilistic error cancellation for obtaining informative (though biased) estimates, and that they validate these theoretical guarantees on real hardware up to 127 qubits.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-032, C-037, C-038, C-041, C-042, C-004]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study grounds its analysis in a Pauli-Lindblad layered noise model that admits efficient learning of its coefficients and defines a single parameter γ to summarize noise strength, which is then related to experimentally observable layer fidelities that compose multiplicatively across layers. The CVaR-based framework is developed with formal lemmas linking noisy and ideal distributions, explicit bounds on estimator variance, and distribution-specific refinements (e.g., for Bernoulli and normal distributions), and it is systematically extended from diagonal to general Hamiltonians and to practical settings like QAOA, fidelity estimation, and QSVM kernels. The authors emphasize experimental validation on real IBM hardware up to 127 qubits, including constraint-preserving QAOA instances and bootstrapping studies that confirm the predicted variance scaling, and they are transparent about scope by explicitly separating SPAM from the main analysis and by discussing when layer-fidelity-based estimates are conservative compared to fitted effective γ.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-016, C-004]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Error mitigation is explicitly framed as a key strategy to bridge the gap between noisy near-term hardware and fully error-corrected quantum computing, and the authors also note that many variational algorithms effectively treat measurement outcomes as direct candidate solutions in optimization contexts. These broader contextual points motivate their focus on sampling and CVaR-based postprocessing.
    [codes: C-007, C-029]

=== PAPER 3a4b78215cc7 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles derivative pricing by formulating it as the computation of the expectation of the derivative payoff under a given probability measure, and focuses in particular on cases where payoffs (and thus prices) can be negative, which standard QAMC formulations usually avoid by assuming strictly positive payoffs or by splitting positive and negative parts.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-022]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose an alternative pipeline to standard Quantum Accelerated Monte Carlo that combines a direct encoding of the payoff into amplitudes, which retains information about the sign of the expected payoff, with a modified Real Quantum Amplitude Estimation (mRQAE) algorithm capable of reading both the magnitude and sign of the target amplitude via iterative Grover-based amplification; they also describe how their quantum simulation matches classical path probabilities, how they simplify to European payoffs and Black–Scholes one-step dynamics, and how they reduce the number of required quantum registers, in some cases to a single register.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-013, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-031]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper restates that using amplitude estimation within QAMC yields a sampling error scaling of order 1/NQ, leading to a quadratic improvement over classical Monte Carlo, and notes that the overall QAMC algorithm is quadratically better in cost terms; they show that a naïve square-root encoding fails to converge for negative payoffs, while the proposed combination of direct encoding and mRQAE can recover the true (negative) price without extra mechanisms and exhibits reasonable performance on positive-payoff contracts, with mRQAE claimed to be asymptotically more efficient and the overall new methodology described as competitive in terms of speed with current standards.
    [codes: C-011, C-014, C-015, C-021, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly compare QAMC with classical Monte Carlo, arguing that QAMC achieves a quadratic improvement in sampling error and overall cost, and report emulator-based experiments where their alternative methodology is experimentally compared against standard QAMC while retaining these speedups; they also state that the new method is competitive in terms of speed with current standards.
    [codes: C-004, C-014, C-015, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: Several limitations are acknowledged: standard QAMC and naïve square-root encodings effectively assume strictly positive prices and payoffs and require splitting the payoff into positive and negative parts to handle sign, which is presented as a limitation; even with direct encoding, the presence of an outer absolute value still prevents correct estimation for negative expectations. On the hardware side, the authors stress that practical implementation is constrained by state-of-the-art devices: the oracle implementation requires an excessively large number of qubits, Grover-like routine depths are not feasible given current decoherence times, and the total gate count implies gate error requirements beyond current technology. They also remark that, overall, many issues remain to be solved in practice when current hardware constraints are considered.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-016, C-022, C-024, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The conclusions highlight future research directions: developing more efficient state-initialization methods that approximately encode the target probability distribution, designing alternative encodings with different normalizations to reduce truncation effects, and systematically exploring different parameter settings for mRQAE.
    [codes: C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim three main contributions, centered on a novel proposal that combines a direct encoding protocol with the mRQAE algorithm to price derivative products with negative payoffs while retaining QAMC-style speedups and being competitive in terms of speed with existing standards.

=== PAPER 3c93fa52d7f0 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper asks whether quantum algorithms can accelerate the mixing of nonreversible Markov processes by constructing suitable reversibilizations and quantum walk–based reflections, motivated by potential impact across applications including finance. It frames the task as preparing (or approximating) reflections about coherent states corresponding to stationary or "most reversible" distributions of ergodic nonreversible Markov chains.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-012, C-013, C-033]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors develop two quantum-walk-based workflows that use Szegedy-type operators within a Projected Unitary Encoding (PUE) framework to construct approximate reflections through target coherent states. The first method applies generalized quantum singular value transformation (GQSVT) to powers P^k of the nonreversible kernel via its curved discriminant, using an implementable fast-forwarding polynomial to realize the reflection, with performance depending on the multiplicative reversibilization PP*. The second method introduces a geometric reversibilization built from the flat discriminant and uses eigenvalue transformations with a leading-eigenvalue-selection polynomial to approximate a reflection about the most reversible distribution, under a reversibility-on-π-average condition; both methods use classical Markov steps as preprocessing until the chain is "reversible enough," after which the reflection is fed into amplitude amplification or quantum amplitude estimation routines.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-031]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For the first workflow, the authors state that the desired reflection about the stationary state can be constructed in time on the order of √(τ_rev τ) (more formally O(√(τ_rev τ(ε)) log(1/ε))) and give a proposition bounding the circuit cost as O(√(τ_rev τ(ε)) log(1/ε)) uses of Szegedy walk operators, reflecting dependence on the pseudo-spectral gap via the multiplicative reversibilization PP*. For the second workflow, they show that under a reversibility-on-π-average condition, the reflection 2|μ⟩⟨μ|−1 around the most reversible distribution can be prepared in O(γ(Q)^{-1/2} log(1/ε)) uses of the associated quantum walk, where the polynomial degree is O(δ^{-1/2} log(1/ε)), and they provide an explicit overlap bound between the target stationary distribution and the most reversible distribution. They also present structural and illustrative results, including that reversibility-on-π-average can be achieved for j much smaller than the mixing time in a bottleneck example, that random walks on groups make eigenvalues of the flat discriminant close to those of the additive reversibilization, that sufficiently mixed kernels or adjoints can yield constant-cost reflections, and that there exists an example where reflection construction time is exponentially smaller than the mixing time; enabling these results is an implementable fast-forwarding polynomial more efficient than a simple monomial.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-011, C-014, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum runtimes are consistently expressed relative to classical mixing-time and spectral-gap quantities, such as τ(ε) and γ∞(P), implying polynomial (up to quadratic or better) speedups compared with classical Markov chain mixing. The authors argue that their up-to-exponential advantage arises in settings where the time to achieve reversibility on π-average or to construct the reflection is much smaller than the full classical mixing time, and they note that for nonreversible chains the relevant quantum cost is tied to reversibilized kernels (multiplicative or additive), which classically control mixing behavior.
    [codes: C-002, C-014, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-029, C-032, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight that they could not provide a general, easy-to-apply criterion for checking the reversibility-on-π-average condition that underpins the efficiency of their second method, limiting its straightforward use in practice. They also acknowledge a fundamental lower bound: their quantum techniques cannot accelerate processes whose mixing time is essentially the same as the time required to traverse their underlying graph, so no meaningful speedup is possible in such cases.
    [codes: C-038, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: To mitigate the difficulty of verifying the reversibility-on-π-average condition analytically, the authors suggest that future work could explore experimental procedures that estimate the phases of the qubitized walk operators, potentially enabling empirical diagnostics of when their second method is applicable.
    [codes: C-039]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to be the first to systematically construct quantum algorithmic techniques that accelerate nonreversible Markov processes by building approximate reflections from Szegedy quantum walks, going beyond the standard quadratic speedup known for reversible chains to obtain up-to-exponential speedups in certain nonreversible settings. Central contributions include two distinct workflows—one based on GQSVT of powers of the kernel and another based on a newly defined geometric reversibilization via the flat discriminant and leading-eigenvalue-selection polynomials—and analytical conditions under which these methods yield strong speedups.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The work is entirely theoretical, with rigor provided through formal definitions of ergodic nonreversible Markov kernels, time-reversal, spectral gaps, and discriminants, and through propositions that precisely quantify runtime, polynomial degree, and state-overlap bounds. The authors systematically build on the PUE framework for encoding Markov kernels and Szegedy walks, and they support their claims with constructed examples (e.g., metastable chains and random walks on groups) and propositions linking quasi-stationary behavior to discriminant overlaps and reversibility-on-π-average, but they do not provide implementation-level details, empirical benchmarks, or datasets.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Some technical constructs and results provide additional conceptual insight beyond the main algorithmic workflows, such as the characterization of the "most reversible" distribution as the maximizer of a quadratic form involving the flat discriminant and the use of quasi-stationary distributions and local metastability to explain why reversibility-on-π-average can emerge well before global mixing. These elements deepen the theoretical understanding of nonreversible Markov dynamics in relation to quantum walk constructions but do not change the core algorithmic framing.
    [codes: C-025, C-033, C-034]

=== PAPER 3e373f43ba5b (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames multivariate quantum state preparation as a core subroutine for many quantum algorithms, including those for financial instrument pricing and other applications where probability distributions or functions must be encoded in amplitudes. It highlights that generic n‑qubit state preparation is exponentially costly, but structured states whose amplitudes are defined by multivariate functions are practically important and underexplored, especially in higher dimensions. The target is to prepare grid-discretized states whose amplitudes approximate given multivariate functions or distributions.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-019]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose LCU- and block-encoding–based protocols that prepare quantum states whose amplitudes encode multivariate functions using truncated Fourier or Chebyshev series, avoiding heavier subroutines such as arithmetic circuits, QFT, or multivariate QSP. They assume the target function admits a Fourier or Chebyshev expansion, approximate it via interpolation when coefficients are not analytically available, and then use tensor-product bases in multiple dimensions with explicit block-encodings for Fourier and Chebyshev basis functions and linear combination of unitaries to assemble the desired operator. The overall state-preparation algorithm uses ancilla registers, post-selection on zero ancillas, and extends straightforwardly from one to two and arbitrary dimensions, with additional implementation optimizations for Chebyshev and circuit simplifications when the target function factorizes.
    [codes: C-002, C-011, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-034, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper derives asymptotic resource estimates showing that the two-qubit gate count scales as O(d^D + D n log d) for Fourier series and O(d^D + D d n log n) for Chebyshev series, with qubit requirements scaling as O(D n + D log d) for both. They provide general formulas for post-selection success probability and show in examples that success probabilities can be on the order of 8–10%, with convergence behavior depending on the function and basis: Chebyshev approximations for a 2D Ricker wavelet exhibit rapid, supergeometric convergence, while Fourier approximations for a bivariate Student’s t-distribution converge asymptotically like O(1/d) due to derivative discontinuities from periodic extension. Numerical simulations of electron wavefunctions in a 3D Coulomb potential match direct numerical computation to numerical precision, and hardware experiments on Quantinuum H2‑1 prepare bivariate Gaussians using 24 qubits and up to 237 two-qubit gates, achieving success probabilities around 10% and fidelities of 0.986 (uncorrelated) and 0.918 (correlated), with observed gate counts agreeing with the predicted scaling.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-027, C-029, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-042, C-045, C-005]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not present explicit runtime or accuracy comparisons against end‑to‑end classical Monte Carlo or numerical integration algorithms; instead, it focuses on how its quantum resource scaling improves on prior quantum state loading schemes. In particular, relative to an earlier Fourier loader, the proposed method introduces ancilla qubits but is more general and, for large n, reduces the two‑qubit gate count by avoiding a quantum Fourier transform, whereas Walsh-series loading yields shallower circuits but at the cost of additional approximation error affecting success probability. Classical computation appears mainly in preprocessing, where Fourier and Chebyshev coefficients are obtained via fast transforms rather than as direct performance baselines.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-034]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations and caveats: generic n‑qubit state preparation remains exponentially costly, so their methods rely on structured function-defined amplitudes. For Fourier-based approaches, non-periodic target functions require a periodic extension trick that can introduce derivative discontinuities at boundaries, leading to slower convergence such as the observed O(1/d) rate for the bivariate Student’s t example. They note that Walsh-series loading, while shallower, introduces extra approximation error that also degrades post-selection success probability. Hardware experiments face substantial shot-noise-induced fluctuations, requiring smoothing via KDE to meaningfully compare empirical and target distributions, and correlated Gaussian instances are harder, showing larger discrepancies between target and reconstructed densities. These observations underline that both approximation choices (basis and domain handling) and noise/shot limitations constrain current performance.
    [codes: C-008, C-015, C-031, C-032, C-039, C-043, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The conclusions outline several extensions: using different basis functions per dimension in hybrid Fourier–Chebyshev schemes and employing recursive constructions to manage higher-dimensional problems, as well as applying univariate quantum signal processing as a post-processing step to manipulate the matrices produced by their method. They also suggest using QSP-based eigenvalue filtering to define and work with hypersurfaces associated with these block-encoded operators.
    [codes: C-049, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to introduce general methods for preparing quantum states that encode multivariate functions while providing both asymptotic and pragmatic resource analyses tailored to near- and medium-term devices. It emphasizes that, despite the practical importance of multivariate state preparation in domains including financial instrument pricing, this problem has been rarely discussed and presents unique challenges, and positions its combination of Fourier/Chebyshev approximation, block-encoding, and LCU—avoiding QFT and multivariate QSP—as a more general and resource-efficient alternative to previous loaders.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-048]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is framed as both a theoretical and practical study, explicitly analyzing resource requirements asymptotically and in terms of near/medium-term hardware budgets, and validating compiled circuits against predicted scaling. The protocols are built on standard block-encoding and LCU primitives and rely on well-characterized classical preprocessing—Fourier and Chebyshev coefficients computed via FFT-like transforms and interpolation when analytic coefficients are unavailable—making the procedure clearly specified. The authors also employ kernel density estimation to smooth noisy hardware measurement data before comparing to target functions, and they list concrete target families (e.g., Ricker wavelets, Student’s t, electron wavefunctions, Gaussians), which supports reproducibility of the numerical and experimental studies.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-011, C-017, C-021, C-022, C-030, C-034, C-037, C-044, C-048]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Some cross-cutting observations include that smoother target functions yield faster convergence of finite series approximations and that Chebyshev expansions do not require periodicity unlike Fourier expansions, which can provide practical advantages. The authors also note that the generalization from two variables to higher-dimensional cases is conceptually straightforward, and that resource-saving tricks are available when controlling certain unitary products in the Chebyshev construction.
    [codes: C-018, C-025, C-028, C-030, C-031]

=== PAPER 3ee4e2ce5b7d (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses high‑dimensional Monte Carlo simulation problems in finance, motivated in particular by credit portfolio loss estimation where the number of obligors – and thus required random numbers – can be on the order of 10^6, creating prohibitive qubit requirements in prior quantum Monte Carlo schemes that allocate a register per random number (C-002, C-003, C-019). It formulates these problems as expectations of integrands that depend on many random variables but can be computed sequentially in Nran steps, a structure that includes credit portfolio risk measurement under a Merton‑type model (C-013, C-023, C-037, C-038). The framing leverages the known quadratic error scaling advantage of quantum Monte Carlo over classical Monte Carlo as the underlying motivation for seeking a more qubit‑efficient implementation (C-001).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-013, C-019, C-023, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum Monte Carlo scheme that effectively performs classical Monte Carlo on a quantum computer: they prepare a uniform superposition over sample indices, then, for each branch, sequentially generate pseudo‑random numbers via a quantum PRNG and update the integrand, finally encoding the sampled integrand value into the amplitude of an ancilla qubit for quantum amplitude estimation (C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-021). Instead of storing all random numbers in parallel registers, they sequentially generate pseudo‑random bit strings on a single PRN register and compute the integrand into another register, which reduces qubit usage at the cost of greater depth (C-004, C-009, C-019). As a concrete PRNG they choose the permuted congruential generator (PCG), whose sequence is realized via linear congruential updates and permutations implemented as modular multiplication, controlled swaps (random rotation), and xorshift using CNOTs, with dedicated gates PPRN and JPRN and an LCG jump‑ahead formula to initialize subsequences (C-006, C-007, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035).
    [codes: C-004, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim that their PRNG‑based quantum Monte Carlo procedure yields the same estimation result as classical Monte Carlo but with quadratic speedup in terms of oracle calls, preserving the O(N^{-1}) error scaling of amplitude estimation compared with the O(N^{-1/2}) scaling of classical Monte Carlo (C-001, C-005, C-027). They decompose the total error into sampling error, which scales as the inverse square root of the number of samples Nsamp, and amplitude‑estimation error, which decreases inversely with the number of oracle calls, showing how both contribute to the final estimation accuracy (C-024, C-025, C-026). For their PCG implementation, they report that the dominant resource cost comes from modular multiplication, which scales linearly in qubits and quadratically in circuit depth with the bit‑length n (C-036). In a small simulator demonstration on a toy multivariable integral, they observe that the quantum estimate closely matches the sampled average over PRNG‑generated points, as intended (C-041, C-045, C-049).
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-036, C-041, C-045, C-049]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The method is explicitly compared with classical Monte Carlo: the authors emphasize that classical Monte Carlo samples only a subset of all possible random‑number patterns and approximates the true expectation Etrue with a simple arithmetic mean Esamp, whereas their quantum procedure reproduces this same Esamp but with quadratic speedup via amplitude estimation (C-010, C-011, C-005). They analytically contrast error scalings, showing that classical Monte Carlo’s error is proportional to N_orac^{-1/2}, while the quantum approach achieves an error term that scales as N_orac^{-1}, leading to a claimed quadratic improvement in oracle complexity (C-001, C-024, C-027, C-028). They also note that previous quantum Monte Carlo methods targeted the true expectation Etrue directly using parallel random‑number registers, providing a conceptual baseline for their qubit‑reduced, Esamp‑oriented scheme (C-019, C-029).
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-010, C-011, C-019, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors stress that their approach relies on the assumption that the integrand can be written in a sequential form in Nran steps, and explicitly acknowledge that not all functions fit this assumption, limiting the method’s applicability beyond cases like credit portfolio loss (C-013, C-022, C-023). They point out a circuit‑design constraint: modular multiplication in the PRNG must be implemented in a self‑updating fashion to avoid outputting to an extra register, otherwise qubit usage would increase and undermine the intended reduction (C-033). They further recognize that the proposed qubit reduction inevitably increases circuit depth, and argue that such deep circuits will not be performable on near‑term quantum hardware without full quantum error correction, which they do not expect to be available soon (C-050, C-051). In their simulator demonstration, they also concede that the very small‑scale PRNG and limited number of samples raise statistical concerns about the robustness of the estimate, framing that example as a proof‑of‑concept rather than a statistically strong validation (C-041, C-048).
    [codes: C-013, C-022, C-023, C-033, C-041, C-048, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: As a mitigation strategy for the depth–qubit trade‑off, the authors suggest partially parallelizing the PRNG: instead of fully sequential generation of all Nran random numbers, they propose generating Nran/n pseudo‑random sequences in parallel, each of length n, and computing corresponding parts of the integrand one‑by‑one, which interpolates between full qubit reduction and full parallelization (C-052).
    [codes: C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s main contribution is a qubit‑reduction strategy for quantum Monte Carlo that replaces the standard one‑register‑per‑random‑number design with a sequential quantum pseudo‑random number generator, allowing the same sampled expectation Esamp as classical Monte Carlo to be estimated with quadratic speedup while using significantly fewer qubits (C-002, C-004, C-005, C-009, C-019, C-021). A second aspect of novelty is the concrete proposal to use the permuted congruential generator on a quantum circuit, chosen because its combination of LCG and bit permutations offers advantages in both required qubit number (memory) and circuit depth, along with explicit gate‑level constructions of the needed PRNG operations (C-006, C-007, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035). The application of this framework to credit portfolio loss under the Merton model, justified by the sequential structure of the loss computation, is presented as an illustrative financial use‑case of the general method (C-023, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040).
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-019, C-021, C-023, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper provides a step‑by‑step description of the quantum algorithm, including preparation of the sample superposition, PRNG subsequence initialization with JPRN, sequential PRNG and integrand updates, and final amplitude encoding, as well as a detailed gate‑level construction for PCG and the credit‑loss circuit, which enhances conceptual transparency (C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-044). For the simulator experiment, they describe a simple multivariable integral, approximate it using PRN‑sampled grid points, and use likelihood‑based amplitude estimation, but also directly acknowledge that the experiment relies on a very small LCG and small sample size, flagging statistical concerns and underscoring the proof‑of‑concept nature rather than a rigorous benchmark (C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049).
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The requirement to convert uniform pseudo‑random numbers into target distributions, such as normal variables needed in many financial models, is noted as an additional step in the integrand computation, and while treated as implementable, it is not deeply analyzed in terms of quantum resource overhead (C-020).

=== PAPER 3f4c5ad6749d (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets quantum pricing of a single-asset European-style option, motivated by the cost of classical Monte Carlo simulations for estimating expected option returns. It formulates the problem as preparing the probability distribution of the asset price at maturity on a quantum register and then computing the expected payoff within this representation, with a focus on designing an efficient way to load this distribution as a prerequisite for quantum speedups over Monte Carlo.
    [codes: C-001, C-010, C-012, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a three-part quantum option-pricing algorithm using a unary encoding where exactly one qubit in the register is in state |1⟩ per basis element: (1) a low-depth amplitude loading circuit that prepares the asset-price distribution at maturity using partial-SWAP gates whose angles encode time dependence, (2) a payoff computation step implemented with simple controlled-Ry gates that map the payoff into the probability of measuring an ancilla qubit, and (3) a standard amplitude estimation stage with a simplified oracle and reflection operator S0 constructed from only a few gates. The unary layout assumes qubits arranged on a 1D line with two-local interactions and can benefit from hardware that natively supports partial-iSWAP-like interactions.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-014, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-004, C-022, C-023, C-005, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The unary representation is reported to substantially simplify circuit structure, yielding low and time-independent depth for distribution loading (⌊n/2⌋+1) and overall O(n) partial-SWAP and O(κn) controlled-Ry gates, as well as a simplified S0 operator in amplitude estimation. In noisy simulations with depolarizing and readout errors, the unary scheme achieves about an order-of-magnitude lower KL divergence than the binary algorithm for the same tolerated error in distribution loading, and shows smaller deviation from the mean payoff estimate, with amplitude estimation reducing payoff uncertainty over iterations. The authors also observe that with around 50 bins, classical discretization errors in the option price can already be brought below about 0.5%, suggesting that moderate bin counts suffice for accurate pricing, and they find that the unary algorithm is more robust to low noise levels than the binary counterpart for several AE iterations.
    [codes: C-006, C-016, C-019, C-025, C-030, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum approach is positioned against classical Monte Carlo, which is characterized as computationally costly for estimating expected option returns, and the use of amplitude estimation is said to offer a quadratic reduction in the number of required quantum circuit runs compared to classical Monte Carlo samples, conditional on efficient distribution loading. Additionally, the study compares unary and binary quantum encodings rather than directly to classical methods, using error maps and KL divergence, and notes that with roughly 50 bins classical discretization error in option prices can already be below 0.5%, providing a classical accuracy reference point.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that unary encoding incurs linear qubit overhead, requiring linearly many qubits in the number of bins and offering lower precision than binary encoding for a fixed qubit budget. They note that readout on all qubits is necessary to enable the post-selection error-mitigation scheme, and that post-selection itself discards an increasing fraction of shots as the number of bins grows, which can erode the effective sampling rate and must be controlled to preserve any quantum advantage. The approach further depends on having an efficient way to load the asset-price probability distribution; without such state preparation, the quadratic speedup from amplitude estimation cannot be realized. On the simulation side, they use a depolarizing-noise model and explicitly neglect thermal relaxation and dephasing, justifying this by the shallow circuit depths and short execution times relative to coherence times, but this is presented as a modelling simplification. They also indicate that the binary approach demands non-local chip connectivity, which is a practical hardware limitation for that baseline rather than for unary itself.
    [codes: C-008, C-012, C-015, C-026, C-034, C-035, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-029]

In clustering, they observe instability with outliers exhibiting extremely large total depths, but show that using universal parameter scaling across instances both improves scaling coefficients and keeps success probabilities for the optimal solution on average above 0.1, which they argue would, if constant, imply algebraic (subexponential) median quantum runtime.

These Markov‑controlled circuits are then embedded into application‑specific architectures: a static credit‑risk state‑preparation circuit with regime‑dependent default probabilities; an option‑pricing circuit with Brownian, price, and payoff registers plus regime‑controlled price updates; and a dynamic portfolio circuit combining a Markov chain, a QFT‑based growth register, and rescaled loss encoding, with MLAE adopted as a near‑term alternative to canonical QAE.

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On real hardware (IBM torino and Honeywell H1), the authors show that their Markov‑chain state‑preparation circuits achieve low mean squared error (MSE), with accuracy improving for larger transition probabilities and error growth mainly driven by the exponential increase in bins and reduced effective shots. For the static regime‑dependent credit‑risk application and regime‑switching derivative pricing, they report MSE tables for specific parameter choices and observe that one‑hot encoding is preferable up to moderate state counts on current IBM hardware. === PAPER 41a852fada38 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the challenge of representing and analyzing continuous-time stochastic processes (CTSPs) on quantum computers for applications in option pricing and insurance, where analytic solutions for stochastic differential equations are often unavailable and classical numerical methods like Monte Carlo can be computationally demanding. The authors specifically identify two unresolved challenges: efficient quantum state preparation for CTSPs and quantum methods for extracting expectations of weighted path integrals and history-sensitive quantities such as first-hitting times, which are central to quantitative finance and actuarial applications. They instantiate the problem in financial contexts including option pricing under the Merton Jump Diffusion model and ruin probability in the Collective Risk Model, and also highlight the need to extract path-dependent information based on whole trajectory histories.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-034, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a two-stage quantum framework for CTSPs consisting of a data preparation (state preparation) procedure and an information extraction procedure. They introduce two quantum representations for continuous-time stochastic processes (QCTSPs), with associated state preparation methods that reduce qubit counts, improve flexibility, and increase sensitivity to discontinuous jumps; these methods exploit an observation about holding times to design circuits with reduced depth and gate complexity and achieve exponential resource reductions in a key parameter called the average holding time τ_avg. The information extraction stage extends quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo to continuous time by evaluating weightless and time-weighted integrals via Riemann-like decompositions and "directed areas" and by adding sequences of flag qubits to extract history-sensitive quantities such as first-hitting times and path-dependent payoffs, yielding a Monte Carlo-style quantum algorithm with quadratic acceleration. The framework is designed so that the data preparation can also serve as a reusable submodule to alleviate input bottlenecks in other quantum algorithms, and its resource requirements are characterized in terms of time horizon T and process memory length, with specific preparation circuits and scaling bounds derived for several process families (e.g., memory-less exponential holding times, Lévy, Poisson, compound Poisson, continuous Markov, and Cox processes).
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The key technical result is that the proposed data preparation achieves exponential reductions in both space and time complexity with respect to a crucial CTSP feature parameter, concretely instantiated as an exponential reduction in the number of state-space copies from O(T)=O(n·τ_avg) under uniform sampling to O(n·ln τ_avg) under their QCTSP method. For memory-less holding times, they show that the holding time τ_j, which is exponentially distributed, can be prepared using ⌈log(−1/(λ_j ln ε))⌉ qubits with constant circuit depth, and more broadly they claim efficient preparation schemes for Lévy, Poisson, compound Poisson, continuous Markov, and Cox processes, with explicit qubit and circuit-depth scalings provided for each. On the extraction side, they claim a quadratic acceleration over classical Monte Carlo for continuous-time simulations by decoding compressed information via their extended quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo, including efficient evaluation of weightless and time-weighted path integrals and history-sensitive quantities via flag qubits. Application results indicate that their quantum CTSP simulation for option pricing under the Merton Jump Diffusion model is consistent with a 40-term truncated Merton formula and with classical Monte Carlo, and they further connect ruin probability in the Collective Risk Model to their general discounted-penalty framework as a special case.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-017, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors position their method as addressing the high storage and computation demands of classical Monte Carlo for CTSPs by compressing process information and then performing quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo with a quadratic speedup in sample complexity or runtime relative to classical Monte Carlo. They explicitly compare their QCTSP-based simulation for Merton Jump Diffusion option pricing against both a truncated analytic Merton formula and classical Monte Carlo, reporting consistent results, and they contrast their QCTSP resource requirements with those of a classical uniform time-sampling scheme, claiming an exponential reduction in the number of state-space copies. More generally, they describe their approach as an extension of quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo to the continuous-time setting and as a potential subroutine to mitigate classical-like data input bottlenecks in other quantum algorithms.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-006, C-010, C-030, C-031, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that prior work has not fully resolved the CTSP state preparation problem or the design of quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo methods capable of handling expectations of weighted integrals and history-sensitive information such as first-hitting times, motivating their contributions but also indicating that the broader problem space remains only partially addressed. They further observe that state preparation complexity grows with the memory length of the process, implying that processes with long memory may be harder to treat with their framework. In their conclusion they explicitly state that they have not explored preparation techniques for several other financially relevant CTSPs, including Hawkes processes, flagging these unaddressed process classes as a limitation of the current work.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-020, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work identified by the authors includes extending their preparation techniques to additional continuous-time stochastic processes of financial relevance, such as Hawkes processes, and more broadly exploring CTSP families with richer memory structures where preparation complexity is higher. Implicitly, the unresolved aspects of quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo for complex history-sensitive functionals suggest further research on more general extraction schemes and on scaling their framework to a wider class of path-dependent financial products and insurance contracts.
    [codes: C-013, C-020, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to introduce an algorithmic quantum framework for continuous-time stochastic processes that integrates compressed data preparation with an extended quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo information extraction stage, offering exponential reductions in key resource parameters and a quadratic acceleration for continuous-time Monte Carlo relative to classical methods. Novel aspects include two general QCTSP encoding schemes with preparation circuits tailored to holding-time structures, enabling exponential resource savings and sensitivity to discontinuous jumps, and a flag-qubit-based method for extracting history-sensitive path information such as first-hitting times, which the authors emphasize as essential for path-dependent option pricing and actuarial computations. They also highlight the breadth of application across statistics, physics, time-series analysis, and finance, with financial and actuarial case studies—Merton Jump Diffusion option pricing and ruin probability in the Collective Risk Model—framing their contribution as introducing quantum computation into aspects of insurance mathematics.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is primarily theoretical and algorithmic, providing resource bounds and circuit constructions for QCTSP preparation and extraction but reporting results via analysis and simulations rather than hardware experiments. They validate their Merton Jump Diffusion option pricing example by comparing QCTSP-based simulations against a truncated analytic formula and classical Monte Carlo, indicating consistency but without detailing datasets or empirical error distributions in the provided excerpts. [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as solving general time-dependent PDEs via a variational principle and then instantiates this for financial derivative pricing, specifically the multi-asset Black–Scholes PDE for European options on many correlated assets, motivated by overcoming the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional settings where fine-grained state information is required.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-033, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a quantum-inspired variational Monte Carlo framework closely related to VQAs, parameterizing the PDE solution as a positive, normalized neural-network quantum state with an autoregressive factorization and sampling from |ψβ(x)|² for importance sampling, on a meshed spatial grid that is digitized into an n‑qubit state; evolution proceeds via stochastic estimation of overlaps under a time-dependent variational principle, with pretraining to match initial conditions and SVD-regularized linear solves.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-032, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For diffusion (heat equation) benchmarks, the variational method produces solutions that match the forward Euler baseline well, though discrepancies grow with spatial dimension; larger Monte Carlo batch sizes substantially reduce relative error. Runtime analysis shows the overall method scaling polynomially with problem size but dominated by the autoregressive sampling cost. Qualitative visualizations indicate that the scheme respects periodic boundary conditions. In Black–Scholes option-pricing experiments, the algorithm is applied across various one- and two-dimensional option types and parameter settings and is reported to achieve satisfactory and robust performance, with particular value claimed in higher-dimensional cases where classical schemes struggle.
    [codes: C-021, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classically, the approach is compared primarily against finite-difference forward Euler and, in 1D Black–Scholes, analytic solutions: for the diffusion benchmarks the authors state that their solution matches forward Euler well but with increasing discrepancy in higher dimensions, and for option pricing they compare to both forward Euler and analytic ground truth in 1D and to forward Euler in 2D. They also emphasize that their formalism parallels finite elements, but classical finite-element methods suffer an exponential problem-size scaling with dimension that their variational approach aims to avoid.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-032, C-034, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors note that although the formalism is applicable to general time-dependent PDEs, their numerical experiments are restricted to inhomogeneous linear cases. They highlight that classical finite-element approaches suffer from an exponential scaling in dimension, which is part of their motivation but also a point of comparison, and in the financial context they stress that all numerical algorithms including theirs require artificial truncation of the spatial domain, introducing a modeling caveat. They also empirically observe that errors grow with the dimensionality of the problem, indicating degradation in accuracy for higher-dimensional PDEs.

=== PAPER 479092dfcc1c (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the bottleneck as the prohibitive number of measurements required for expectation value estimation in hybrid quantum–classical algorithms such as VQE, and notes that expectation estimation is likewise a core subroutine for many non‑variational quantum algorithms. The authors argue that realizing quantum advantage for such tasks will require methods that dramatically reduce this measurement cost.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a family of engineered likelihood function (ELF) schemes for expectation (amplitude) estimation that are inspired by quantum metrology, phase estimation, and α‑VQE, and explicitly constructed to be robust to noise and not require ancilla qubits. The core idea is to use generalized reflections in circuits that keep the state within a two‑dimensional subspace, thereby shaping the likelihood via Chebyshev‑type and more general trigono‑multiquadratic forms, and then performing approximate Bayesian inference using Gaussian moment matching and local sinusoidal approximations, with circuit parameters optimized by minimizing posterior variance or maximizing Fisher information and its low‑fidelity slope proxy.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-009, C-013, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-032, C-033, C-043]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Analytically, the ELF framework is shown to enhance information gain per sample, with Fisher information growing quadratically in circuit depth in the idealized regime and yielding a runtime model that interpolates between Heisenberg (O(1/ε)) and shot‑noise (O(1/ε²)) scaling. The authors identify and then mitigate noise‑induced ‘dead spots’ in the likelihood, showing that under their noise model the ELF bias is simply rescaled by a fidelity factor and that Fisher information can serve as a good proxy for variance reduction and inverse‑MSE growth. Simulation studies indicate that ELF generally outperforms Chebyshev likelihood functions (CLF), that ancilla‑free schemes are superior to ancilla‑based ones, that ELF performance is stable across true parameter values, that higher layer fidelity monotonically improves performance, and that deeper circuits do not always help, with performance depending on a balance between circuit power and accumulated noise.
    [codes: C-005, C-008, C-010, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-024, C-026, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-046]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper compares engineered likelihood functions against conventional, Chebyshev‑derived likelihoods (CLF), arguing that the quantum‑generated ELF cannot be reproduced by classical post‑processing of repeated samples and thus represents a non‑classical sampling primitive. Empirically, the authors report that ELF’s Fisher information exceeds that of CLF for most parameter values and that in both ancilla‑free and ancilla‑based settings ELF performs as well as or better than CLF, while also explaining that CLF can fail near ‘dead spots’ in its likelihood landscape where Fisher information collapses.
    [codes: C-006, C-010, C-012, C-015, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-038, C-045]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors highlight that likelihood calibration is a critical but unresolved practical issue: efficiently learning nuisance parameters in the likelihood models will be essential, and miscalibration can introduce systematic bias in parameter estimates. They also stress a hardware‑level limitation that the benefits of error correction and improved gate fidelities must outweigh the longer estimation runtimes implied by error‑corrected circuits. Additionally, they acknowledge that deeper circuits do not necessarily yield better estimation performance because of a nontrivial tradeoff among circuit depth, noise accumulation, and statistical power, implying that ELF performance is sensitive to hardware noise characteristics and depth choices.
    [codes: C-041, C-042, C-047, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper proposes several future directions, including investigating analytical upper and lower bounds on estimation performance for engineered likelihoods and rigorously establishing how much ELFs can increase worst‑case inverse‑variance rates compared with conventional likelihoods. The authors also point to the need for better methods for efficient likelihood function calibration in realistic noisy devices.
    [codes: C-045, C-048, C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main novelty claim is the introduction of the engineered likelihood function (ELF) framework, which uses quantum signal‑processing ideas and tunable generalized reflections to shape likelihoods, boost Fisher information per sample, and remove noise‑induced dead spots without requiring ancilla qubits. The authors further claim that this framework provides a unified, hardware‑aware runtime model that smoothly connects NISQ‑regime performance to error‑corrected Heisenberg‑limit scaling, and that the resulting likelihoods appear to be beyond the reach of classical sampling and post‑processing.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is primarily theoretical and simulation‑based, with a detailed analytical treatment of Fisher information and runtime via Chebyshev‑type bounds and information‑theoretic arguments. The authors design optimization procedures (gradient and coordinate ascent) that exploit an O(L) evaluation cost for relevant coefficients in the trigono‑multiquadratic ELF structure, and they use approximate Bayesian updating via Gaussian moment matching and local sinusoidal fits to make inference tractable. They validate their heuristic performance predictions by showing that estimated inverse‑MSE growth rates roughly match empirical simulation results, and they explicitly analyze how performance varies with layer fidelity and circuit depth, emphasizing the need to balance depth, noise, and statistical power.
    [codes: C-010, C-012, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-033, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors connect their approach to prior work by noting that Bayesian phase estimation can exhibit quantum advantages in noisy settings, and they reiterate that expectation value estimation is a key building block for many high‑impact, non‑variational quantum algorithms, though they do not specialize these observations to any specific financial application within this paper.
    [codes: C-006, C-007]

=== PAPER 48cd8220e3b2 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the foundational task of preparing quantum states that encode classical data, focusing on amplitude-encoding smooth real functions and, as a key special case, probability distributions relevant to finance (including α‑stable/Lévy distributions) on a binary grid of N qubits. The problem is framed as understanding and exploiting entanglement structure in the matrix product state (MPS) representation of these discretized functions to design shallow, accurate encoding circuits for Monte Carlo–style financial simulations.
    [codes: C-001, C-013, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use an MPS-based state-preparation approach: discretize the target function on a binary grid, represent it as an MPS, analyze and truncate bond dimensions based on entanglement measures (purity and entropy), and then synthesize shallow "double-staircase"/V-layer circuits from these MPS isometries. They further optimize the method via a greedy disentangling procedure whose origin can be shifted, introduce a truncation threshold ε_trunc to decide which two-qubit gates to include, make a central gate variational in subsequent layers, and exploit a two-CNOT synthesis for generic isometries. For scalability, Tensor Cross Interpolation (TCI) is used to build the MPS directly from a computable PDF without storing the full state vector, with black-box access to the function and complexity O(Nχ²).
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main theoretical results are rigorous asymptotic expansions for entanglement in the MPS representation of smooth functions: purities and entanglement entropies across bonds decay exponentially with bond index k, with leading corrections controlled by derivative-based functionals g₁(f) and eigenvalues of reduced density matrices scaling as O(1/4^{k n}), and a 2^{-k} scaling for the first subleading spectrum component. These analyses yield universal scaling relations for smooth functions and show how localization and support affect entanglement—for example, delta-peaked distributions are unentangled while power-law (heavy-tailed) distributions are more entangled than exponentially decaying ones—and improve previous bounds by showing the first nonvanishing term in purity scales as 1/4^k. From these spectra, the authors derive analytical functionals to predict fidelity of single-layer circuits, including corrections for localization, and report that even one-layer circuits can achieve infidelity ≤10⁻³ on smooth distributions, with analytic fidelity estimates from truncated singular values agreeing well with numerics. Empirically, they validate the method on heavy-tailed α‑stable/Lévy and other finance-relevant distributions, including on IBM devices up to 64 qubits, where distributions often pass Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests or at least qualitatively match the target at utility scale, while TCI-based preprocessing achieves very small classical relative errors with O(Nχ²) function evaluations.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical comparison is implicit rather than explicit: the authors note that generic functions can require exponentially large MPS bond dimension, whereas for polynomials and smooth functions the entanglement-based analysis shows much more favorable scaling, enabling shallow quantum circuits; and via TCI they contrast O(Nχ²) black-box function evaluations with the 2^N cost of naively constructing full state vectors. However, they do not report direct empirical performance comparisons against concrete classical baselines for financial simulation or distribution sampling.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-018, C-031, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations and conditions: generically, functions may require exponentially large MPS bond dimensions, so their favorable entanglement scaling is restricted to smooth (or sufficiently regular) functions. Their asymptotic expansions hold only beyond a scale set by the function’s characteristic length (k > log₂(1/2σ)), and for functions with only finitely many absolutely continuous derivatives, the universal entanglement results apply only up to order r+1 in the spectrum. They further show that large-scale, coarse qubit regimes exhibit non-universal entanglement behavior that depends on concentration/localization, meaning performance is function-class dependent. On real hardware, noise creates a depth–accuracy trade-off where theoretically better but deeper circuits can perform worse than shallower ones, and at the very largest circuit sizes the prepared distributions no longer pass quantitative statistical tests, even though they retain qualitative features.
    [codes: C-009, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-040, C-044]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper suggests extending the density-matrix and entanglement analysis from univariate to multivariate functions, which would be necessary for higher-dimensional financial models, and calls for a more detailed study of hardware noise effects on function preparation, beyond the preliminary depth–noise trade-off observations presented.
    [codes: C-045, C-046]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed novelties are the derivation of rigorous, universal entanglement scaling laws for smooth functions in their MPS representation, including explicit asymptotic formulas for purities, entanglement entropies, and reduced density eigenvalues that improve exponentially over prior bounds; the identification of how smoothness, localization, and support shape these spectra (e.g., unentangled delta peaks versus more entangled heavy tails); and the construction of an improved MPS-based algorithm for shallow, accurate encoding circuits, including V-layer architecture, fidelity functionals, and TCI-based scalable MPS construction that together enable utility-scale circuits for heavy-tailed financial distributions. They emphasize that their analytic expansions lead directly to functionals controlling the fidelity of approximate encoding circuits and to a more efficient, compute- and memory‑efficient pipeline.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-011, C-012, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-037, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study is grounded in a formal density-matrix and entanglement framework, using purity and entropy as quantitative measures to guide bond truncation and circuit synthesis. The authors analytically connect truncated singular values to fidelity for single-layer circuits and validate these predictions against numerical simulations, including corrections for localization that match numerics across all tested supports. They perform both ideal and noisy simulations and run circuits on IBM hardware up to 64 qubits, validating distributions using standard statistics like Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests; for cases where the tests fail at very large scales, they still assess qualitative agreement. The use of TCI is presented with clear complexity scaling and without requiring explicit storage of 2^N amplitudes, and the circuit synthesis details (V-layer shape, truncation hyperparameter, variational gate, two‑CNOT isometry decomposition) are described enough to suggest reproducibility, though full implementation details or open-source code are not explicitly mentioned in the coded excerpts.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-006, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The code noting that exponentially decaying functions are less entangled than power-law–tailed ones further illustrates how entanglement reflects function class and aligns with the financial motivation to handle heavy-tailed distributions, but it does not introduce additional methodological or limitation content beyond what is already captured in other dimensions.
    [codes: C-030]

=== PAPER 49aaab8109ac (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses Monte Carlo integration (MCI) for estimating expectations of functions of random variables, focusing on problems where a probability distribution is encoded in a quantum state and one wants the mean of a (possibly multivariate) function of the samples, including products and correlations. The authors emphasise that, in principle, the mean of any function applied to the samples can be estimated and explicitly consider expectations of products of functions of two correlated random variables as a target quantity.
    [codes: C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-023, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The method is a variant of quantum Monte Carlo integration based on encoding a (possibly multivariate) discrete probability distribution into a quantum state |p⟩ and then using a Fourier series decomposition of the function applied to samples, with each Fourier component estimated by a quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) subroutine. The approach employs a periodic, piecewise extension of the target function to enable this Fourier expansion, uses a single bank of rotation gates to build the amplitude-encoding circuit with minimal depth, and estimates cosine and sine expectations via specially parameterised QAE calls; the authors also extend this to products of functions of two variables via a double Fourier expansion and trigonometric identities that reduce products of sines and cosines to single terms.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-008, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-024, C-025]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main theoretical result is that the expectation of a suitably smooth function (and of products of functions of two correlated random variables) can be estimated with mean-squared error in Θ(q^−λ) using q calls to the state-preparation circuit, thereby preserving the full quadratic quantum advantage in query complexity while keeping circuit depth minimal. The analysis shows that, under the Fourier-based scheme, the total number of queries remains proportional to the target query budget, and numerical simulations indicate that the Fourier QMCI method outperforms both classical MCI and a rescaled QMCI approach at sufficiently small desired RMSE, with an observed RMSE slope of about −1.02 that matches the predicted scaling, albeit with a larger constant factor than conventional QMCI.
    [codes: C-001, C-010, C-017, C-021, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors position their algorithm as retaining the full quadratic speedup in query complexity over classical Monte Carlo integration, and report simulations where Fourier QMCI surpasses classical MCI at low target error levels. They also compare against a rescaled QMCI scheme and conventional QMCI with quantum arithmetic, finding that although Fourier QMCI has a larger constant factor than conventional QMCI, it maintains the asymptotic quadratic advantage while avoiding deep quantum arithmetic circuits.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-007, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper stresses that the quantum speedup is an advantage in query complexity, so any overhead in preparing the probability-encoding state or computing required quantities classically must be accounted for. A key practical obstacle for NISQ devices is that quantum arithmetic (e.g., implementing arcsine) is depth- and qubit-intensive, motivating the authors to avoid it. The rescaled QMCI benchmark they compare against is acknowledged to have a reduced convergence rate and can perform artificially well when the mean lies at the median of the distribution support, so they avoid such cases in their experiments. The method’s theoretical guarantees require smoothness conditions on the target function (continuity, continuous first derivative, and bounded piecewise-continuous second and third derivatives), and the analysis assumes that the convergence behaviour of the chosen QAE subroutine as a function of the number of oracle uses is known. Additionally, they note that if the Fourier coefficients of the extended function cannot be computed symbolically and must instead be obtained by numerical integration, the algorithm may merely shift rather than reduce the overall computational burden.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-012, C-013, C-022, C-028, C-032]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors argue that their low-depth Fourier-based QMCI techniques should have ongoing utility, suggesting they will remain relevant and adaptable as quantum hardware progresses beyond the NISQ era.
    [codes: C-035]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims a QMCI method that simultaneously achieves full quadratic quantum advantage in query complexity, minimal circuit depth by avoiding quantum arithmetic and phase estimation, and applicability to expectations of functions and products of functions of random variables—something the authors state no previous proposal has accomplished in combination. They further emphasise the flexibility of their Fourier-based construction, arguing it can be readily adapted to various real-world settings of interest.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-008, C-010, C-014, C-034]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: For numerical validation, the authors choose a synthetic discrete distribution whose encoding can be prepared by a very shallow circuit, to avoid simulation slowdowns and to align with the low-depth goals of their scheme; they also deliberately avoid distributions whose mean equals the median of the support, because this would make the rescaled QMCI baseline look artificially strong. They show that the fitted RMSE scaling of Fourier QMCI closely matches their theoretical prediction, and they quantify constant-factor differences versus conventional QMCI, while highlighting explicit resource estimates for quantum arithmetic to motivate their design choices. The method’s flexibility and adaptability to various application settings are claimed, though the experiments themselves are confined to a carefully chosen toy distribution.
    [codes: C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Fourier analysis plays a central technical role: the authors rely on the rapid decay (as 1/n³ or faster) of Fourier coefficients under their smoothness assumptions to justify truncation and to distribute the error budget across finitely many Fourier modes when estimating the target expectation. This truncation strategy underpins their query-complexity accounting and connects the analytic properties of the extended function with the quantum resource scaling.
