=== PAPER 8d08019fb608 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper is framed as an extensive survey of how quantum machine learning (QML) can be applied to core quantitative finance problems, including portfolio optimization, market prediction and trading, option pricing, risk measurement (VaR/CVaR), credit risk, and fraud detection as anomaly detection. It motivates these applications by arguing that quantum properties such as superposition and entanglement could improve on traditional financial modelling and ML methods. The authors also carefully define central financial tasks and metrics (e.g., portfolio optimization, Sharpe ratio, VaR/CVaR, credit rating categories, and the treatment of fraud detection as a special case of anomaly detection) to ground the surveyed QML work in standard finance problem formulations.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: As a survey, the paper covers several families of quantum and quantum‑hybrid methods rather than implementing one specific algorithm. It explains basic gate‑model concepts (qubits, superposition, unitary gates) and positions QML within the NISQ era, emphasizing hybrid quantum–classical algorithms where parametrized quantum circuits (QNNs) are trained via classical optimizers. The authors describe key building blocks such as QAOA for combinatorial optimization, QAE for amplitude estimation, HHL for linear systems, and quantum PCA for eigenvalue problems, and then map these to finance use cases (e.g., QAOA and VQE for portfolio optimization, QAE and qGAN-based loading for derivative pricing, quantum kernels and QSVMs for classification and anomaly detection, and quantum GANs and kernel methods for fraud and credit risk). They also highlight architectures such as feature‑map plus variational layers in QNNs and multiple quantum kernel learning schemes used in risk and fraud contexts.
    [codes: C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-053, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064, C-070, C-074, C-075, C-083]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors compile reported results across several financial subdomains. For portfolio optimization, cited work using quantum annealers and variational algorithms reports that optimized reverse annealing can be more than 100× faster than forward annealing, that gate‑model rebalancing on small portfolios is feasible on NISQ devices and can find portfolios within 5% of optimal adjusted returns, and that VQE can yield solutions close to exact ones under suitable hyperparameters. In market prediction and trading, they report studies where quantum deep hedging policies based on QNNs significantly outperform Black–Scholes hedges, quantum‑assisted feature selection improves predictive accuracy with lower dimensionality, quantum Elman networks achieve similar prediction quality with much smaller hidden/context layers, and hybrid deep QNNs demonstrate high forecasting accuracy across regression and extrapolation tasks, including for churn prediction and stock prediction. For pricing, the survey cites evidence that qPCA reduces noisy factors in interest‑rate models, qGAN‑based loading is gate‑efficient, QAE-based methods achieve quadratic or near-quadratic speedups for option pricing, shallow circuits can accurately price European and Asian options, unary encodings may be advantageous on near‑term devices, and several quantum approaches (including on IBM Q hardware) demonstrate quadratic or exponential speedups in steps or dimensionality for Monte Carlo and PDE‑based pricing. In risk management and fraud/credit analytics, the authors report that QAE-based methods offer near‑quadratic speedups for VaR and CVaR estimation, quantum feature selection on real credit risk data can match or surpass state‑of‑the‑art classical methods, quantum kernels can improve average precision as system size grows, QSVMs can deliver lower false positives and higher precision in fraud detection, QBoost offers interpretability benefits over classical boosting, quantum GNNs achieve AUC around 0.85 in graph‑based fraud detection, and quantum GAN and kernel setups show competitive or superior performance on anomaly detection benchmarks.
    [codes: C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064, C-065, C-066, C-067, C-068, C-069, C-070, C-071, C-072, C-076, C-079, C-081, C-084, C-085]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Across the surveyed studies, quantum methods are usually benchmarked against classical baselines. For optimization, the authors describe QA and VQE approaches that come close to or match the performance of existing classical solvers on problems of comparable size, and note that VQE can approximate exact solutions under good hyperparameter choices. In trading and hedging, QNN-based deep hedging strategies reportedly significantly outperform the Black–Scholes hedge, and quantum‑assisted feature selection and QENN architectures match or exceed classical models with fewer parameters. In risk and fraud analysis, QAE‑based VaR/CVaR estimation is claimed to surpass classical Monte Carlo in efficiency, quantum feature selection for credit risk can compete with or surpass state‑of‑the‑art classical methods, quantum kernels can outperform standard approaches in average precision as problem size grows, and QSVMs are reported to have lower false positives and higher precision than both classical and other quantum baselines. Some comparisons are negative or neutral: QSVMs in certain stock prediction experiments do not show clear advantages over classical SVMs, and in a blockchain phishing study no performance improvement is observed when increasing the number of qubits, which tempers expectations of uniform quantum superiority.
    [codes: C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-059, C-060, C-063, C-066, C-067, C-068, C-069, C-071, C-072, C-076, C-079, C-081, C-084, C-085]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges that current quantum hardware and algorithms face substantial limitations that constrain practical impact. At a general level, the authors stress that existing NISQ devices and simulators are still far from demonstrating robust quantum advantage, being restricted by limited qubit counts, noise, and decoherence. They note that scalability, hardware limits, and algorithmic complexity remain overarching challenges. In specific applications, they report that current hardware issues hindered QAOA-based FX reserves management to the point that only a few demonstrations succeeded even for a five-variable problem, and that available QPUs were not sufficiently stable or error‑tolerant for fraud detection at realistic scales. They also highlight more nuanced limitations in QML experiments: QSVMs show no clear performance advantage over classical SVMs in some stock prediction tasks, increased qubit counts did not yield better performance in a blockchain phishing detection setting, and certain speedup claims are theoretical or emulator-based rather than demonstrated on large‑scale, noisy hardware. The discussion of Black–Scholes assumptions and the curse of dimensionality in classical models further contextualizes where quantum methods are intended to help, while implicitly acknowledging that both classical and quantum approaches can be limited by modelling assumptions and high dimensional data.
    [codes: C-014, C-020, C-036, C-037, C-060, C-077, C-078, C-080, C-086]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors argue that overcoming hardware scalability, noise, and algorithmic complexity will be crucial to realize the potential of QML in finance, explicitly calling for continued research on more scalable algorithms and more capable devices. They also point to specific methodological avenues, such as further exploring unary encodings for option pricing which may offer practical advantages on near‑term hardware, and investigating how quantum noise and other QML properties might be harnessed to improve fairness in financial decision systems. The conclusion frames the field as a bidirectional exchange where financial problems can inspire new quantum methods, implicitly encouraging future research at this interdisciplinary interface.
    [codes: C-065, C-082, C-087, C-088]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as an extensive, structured overview of quantum machine learning applications in quantitative finance, spanning portfolio optimization, trading, pricing, risk management, and fraud/anomaly detection. Its contribution lies in synthesizing technical background in finance and ML (e.g., definitions of portfolio optimization, VaR/CVaR, fraud as anomaly detection, feature selection/extraction, and ML evaluation metrics) with the building blocks of quantum and hybrid QML algorithms, then mapping these systematically onto financial use cases. The authors also emphasize the emerging, NISQ‑era perspective on QML and highlight a two‑way relationship where quantitative finance not only benefits from but also inspires the development of quantum methods, which they present as a distinctive framing of the field’s current state.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-031, C-038, C-043, C-088]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the survey dedicates space to explaining standard ML workflows and concepts (training pipeline, curse of dimensionality, feature selection and extraction, supervised/unsupervised/RL paradigms, neural network structures, and evaluation metrics like ROC/AUC), providing readers with the conceptual tools to assess QML studies. In the quantum risk and credit‑risk sections, the authors note papers that explicitly examine scalability and expected runtime, describe precise classifier and metric choices (e.g., logistic regression with log‑loss, average precision, false positives, interpretability), and report experiments on real‑world datasets, including credit risk and fraud detection data. They also mention works that test quantum kernels both in simulation and on real hardware, and a QML fairness verification framework that explores the impact of quantum noise, which signals attention to robustness and ethical aspects beyond raw accuracy. However, because this is a survey, it generally relays other authors’ methodological setups rather than enforcing a unified experimental protocol, and many reported results are drawn from small‑scale or idealized simulations, as suggested by repeated emphasis on NISQ limitations and hardware instability.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-073, C-075, C-082, C-083]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several codes provide core technical or definitional background but are not central to the survey’s comparative or evaluative claims. These include detailed formulations of mean–variance portfolio optimization and constrained/binary variants, the identification of algorithmic trading as quantitative, ML‑driven automation, and specific formal results about quantum subroutines (e.g., QAE, HHL, quantum PCA) that underlie many of the reviewed applications. They contribute to the paper’s pedagogical role rather than to specific findings or limitations.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-045]

=== PAPER 8d8d76478f6b (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the computational bottleneck of Monte Carlo (MC) simulations used in particle‑in‑cell (PIC) codes, where large sample sizes make classical MC very expensive, and explores replacing these with a quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) routine for predicting electron–positron pair yields in head‑on photon–photon collisions via the linear Breit–Wheeler process. The authors formulate the task as estimating the expected number of produced pairs by viewing the Breit–Wheeler cross‑section/probability as a function that can be approximated by a low‑order polynomial and embedded into a quantum circuit for amplitude estimation on a simplified head‑on collision geometry. They explicitly choose the linear Breit–Wheeler process as a testbed because its cross‑section can be approximated by a low‑order polynomial that is convenient for quantum algorithms, while also simplifying geometry (head‑on collisions) to make the problem tractable on current hardware.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-016, C-037, C-046]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed quantum approach is a NISQ‑oriented quantum Monte Carlo integration built around iterative quantum amplitude estimation (IQAE), designed to exploit the quadratic sample‑complexity improvement of amplitude estimation while avoiding the phase‑estimation overhead that makes canonical QAE impractical on NISQ devices. Algorithmically, the workflow consists of four main steps: (1) quantum state preparation of the photon energy distribution using either Qiskit native initialization, a variational CNOT–Ry ring ansatz, or an ancilla‑less Fourier Series Loader (FSL) that loads arbitrary functions via truncated Fourier series; (2) polynomial approximation of the Breit–Wheeler cross‑section and its embedding into an ancilla qubit via controlled Ry rotations, implemented using Qiskit’s PolynomialPauliRotations; (3) iterative amplitude amplification and estimation via IQAE using Chernoff‑Hoeffding bounds to refine confidence intervals; and (4) post‑processing of measured amplitudes into expected pair counts. For real‑hardware demonstrations, the circuit is reduced to a three‑qubit work register initialized by a parametric circuit and Fourier series, executed on a trapped‑ion QPU with reported gate error characteristics.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-032, C-037, C-038, C-049, C-050, C-053, C-054, C-055, C-056, C-058, C-042, C-041, C-048]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On ideal (noise‑free) simulators, the QMC algorithm’s predicted pair counts are described as essentially indistinguishable from analytical theory, with relative error consistently below 1% and a mean accuracy of about 99.8% across state‑preparation strategies; moreover, the authors quantify that the polynomial embedding itself introduces a mean approximation error of about 0.69%. They report that, across different initialization schemes and distribution widths, simulations retain over 99% accuracy, though performance depends on distribution skewness, with their Fourier Series Loader performing worse on negatively skewed distributions than on positively skewed ones. In controlled comparisons with fixed query/sample budgets, they find that the quantum Monte Carlo routine yields improved accuracy over classical Monte Carlo; additionally, they observe that increasing the number of qubits improves resolution and thus accuracy in ideal simulation, and that on a trapped‑ion QPU their implementation achieves over 90% accuracy relative to theory, with hardware trends qualitatively matching ideal‑simulator behavior.
    [codes: C-002, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-022, C-029, C-030, C-040, C-051, C-054, C-033]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly compare their quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) routine against classical Monte Carlo under a fixed query/sample budget, setting classical simulations to have the same sample size as the number of quantum queries, and report that the QMC routine consistently improves upon classical MC in terms of accuracy. They interpret their idealized results as achieving accuracy that exceeds classical Monte Carlo, and they link this performance advantage to the theoretical quadratic reduction in required samples afforded by amplitude estimation relative to classical MC for the same target accuracy.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-027, C-028, C-033, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper stresses that accuracy is ultimately limited by the approximations introduced when embedding polynomials and initializing the quantum state, with the total error decomposed into IQAE estimation error plus approximation error from polynomial fitting and state preparation. Because the Breit–Wheeler cross‑section is complicated, they state there is no simple way to embed the exact function: fully accurate quantum arithmetic would make the circuit too large for current NISQ devices, necessitating low‑degree polynomial approximations that introduce a quantified but non‑zero embedding error. Geometrically, the problem is simplified to ideal head‑on collisions to keep it compatible with current algorithms and hardware, and the authors note that canonical QAE is too expensive for present NISQ hardware, motivating IQAE but also constraining algorithm choice. They highlight that certain state‑preparation methods are hardware‑incompatible or scale poorly: Qiskit’s native initialization uses operations not supported on today’s quantum computers; their variational CNOT–Ry ansatz tends to overfit and misrepresent the initial Gaussian when more qubits are used, struggles beyond six‑qubit work registers, and cannot generate skewed distributions at all. Distribution‑dependent performance limitations are also reported, with the Fourier Series Loader performing worse for negatively skewed distributions, and they acknowledge that limited qubit counts on NISQ devices reduce routine accuracy even though feasibility is demonstrated. Finally, they point out that their current study is restricted to a univariate problem, that more qubits, error correction, and more shots would be required to improve hardware accuracy, and that the circuit used on hardware is reduced to a small three‑qubit work register, implicitly constraining resolution and scalability.
    [codes: C-003, C-016, C-021, C-023, C-026, C-034, C-035, C-048, C-052, C-056, C-059, C-025, C-031, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose extending their currently univariate formulation to multivariable problems, identifying this as a possible avenue to broaden the applicability of their QMC framework. They also outline plans to adapt their quantum Monte Carlo routine to strong‑field QED (SFQED) modules within classical simulation codes, aiming at a meaningful integration between high‑performance classical computing (HPC) and quantum processing units (QPUs). Additionally, they suggest that incorporating error‑correcting algorithms, employing more qubits, and increasing the number of measurement shots could further enhance the accuracy of hardware implementations, and mention broader pathways toward integration with classical simulation codes as a key development direction.
    [codes: C-005, C-031, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as a NISQ‑hardware‑conscious quantum Monte Carlo integration scheme for linear Breit–Wheeler pair production that combines approximate polynomial embedding of the cross‑section, flexible state‑preparation methods (including a Fourier Series Loader capable of initializing arbitrary functions without ancillas), and iterative quantum amplitude estimation into a four‑step workflow tailored for current devices. The authors emphasize that, under ideal simulation, this composite algorithm attains accuracy exceeding classical Monte Carlo at the same query budget, and they present a proof‑of‑principle implementation on a trapped‑ion QPU that achieves over 90% accuracy relative to theory despite limited resources, suggesting near‑term feasibility and a pathway to hybrid HPC–QPU integration for expensive Monte Carlo workloads.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-006, C-008, C-011, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-053, C-054, C-029, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper provides a structured four‑step description of its QMC routine—state preparation, ancilla‑based probability embedding, amplitude estimation, and post‑processing—summarizing how it is built upon modular sub‑algorithms and explicitly decomposing total error into IQAE and approximation components. The authors carefully motivate and quantify their polynomial approximation of the Breit–Wheeler cross‑section, report the mean embedding error, and discuss how increasing the number of qubits refines resolution and improves accuracy under ideal simulation, while also characterizing failure modes such as variational overfitting and hardware‑incompatible initialization. For hardware experiments, they document key device characteristics (number of physical qubits, connectivity, and gate error rates), the reduced three‑qubit circuit design, and the consistent use of a fixed shot count, and note that hardware results qualitatively follow ideal‑simulator trends, all of which contribute to understanding experimental rigour and the constraints on reproducibility.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also summarizes relevant physical background for the linear Breit–Wheeler process, including the threshold condition for pair production and the behavior of the cross‑section—such as its decrease at high center‑of‑mass energy s, which reduces pair‑production probability—providing physical context for the quantum simulations.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a core practical obstacle for quantum algorithms that rely on classical data: exact amplitude-encoding circuits are often exponentially deep in qubit count and can dominate the usable circuit depth on NISQ devices, limiting overall algorithm performance. Instead of assessing embeddings in isolation, the authors focus on how approximate, compressed data embeddings affect the performance of full downstream algorithms (e.g., Grover, amplitude estimation, QFT) and note that the sensitivity of final results to embedding quality is non-obvious and may depend on algorithm family, data complexity, and chosen fidelity metrics. They reference prior AAE work applied to financial marker calculations as a motivating use case for finance-relevant applications of such approximate loading schemes.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-014]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study investigates approximate amplitude encoding via variational compression: a variational quantum circuit is trained to reproduce a target amplitude-encoded state, thereby compressing standard deep data-loading circuits. The work is conducted in a noiseless statevector setting and is structured in two parts: (1) training various VQC ansaetze to approximate target data states under different input distributions, and (2) running standard algorithms—amplitude amplification (Grover), amplitude estimation, and QFT—on these approximate input states to assess impact on final-state fidelity. Four ansaetze are compared for the compression task (no entanglement, Walsh–Hadamard + CZ + RX, RY–CNOT, and a hardware-efficient ansatz), with RY–CNOT singled out for downstream benchmarking; training data include uniform-with-noise, periodic signals (sparse sine-wave superpositions), and random normal amplitudes, and standard MQT Bench implementations are used for the benchmark circuits with fidelity to ideal amplitude encoding as the main comparison metric.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-013, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors find that for generic data and small qubit counts, amplitude-encoding circuits can be substantially depth-compressed with only marginal loss in state fidelity, with at least a factor-of-two depth reduction causing less than 0.01% loss in final-state fidelity and up to fivefold compression achievable when allowing input-state infidelities below about 5%. Among the tested ansaetze, the RY–CNOT ansatz offers the best trade-off between approximation fidelity and depth compression for real-valued data, and the required number of layers grows sub-exponentially rather than exponentially with the number of qubits, with compression potential increasing as circuit size grows. For high-fidelity approximations (above roughly 95%), the studied downstream algorithms do not further worsen the input-state infidelity, and certain algorithms—notably the quantum Fourier transform—appear robust or even self-correcting to high-fidelity input approximations, consistent with the interpretation that QFT can act as a high-frequency noise filter.
    [codes: C-009, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-010, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not report any explicit empirical or complexity-theoretic comparison to classical data-loading or classical financial algorithms; it restricts itself to comparing exact versus approximate quantum data encodings and their impact on quantum algorithm performance.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly confine their analysis to a noiseless setting and acknowledge that understanding the effect of realistic hardware noise both on VQC training and on executing algorithms with approximate embeddings remains an open question for practical deployment. They also note that their conclusions are based on a limited set of algorithm families and embedding schemes, and that the dependence of final outputs on embedding quality is complex and may vary with algorithm type, data complexity, and the fidelity metric, implying that their current robustness observations are not yet systematically generalized.
    [codes: C-005, C-016, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose that reducing data-encoding depth via variational compression could enable execution of substantially larger algorithms on NISQ hardware with limited quantum volume, and they argue that a systematic classification of quantum algorithms by robustness to input-data compression would be of practical value. They suggest extending the study to additional algorithm families and alternative embedding schemes, as well as rigorously investigating how hardware noise affects both VQC training and the performance of algorithms using approximate embeddings.
    [codes: C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is positioned as a systematic study of how variationally compressed amplitude encodings affect full quantum algorithms, shifting focus from optimizing approximate embeddings in isolation to the performance of the compound algorithm. Within this framework, the paper introduces a comparative evaluation of several VQC ansaetze for approximate amplitude encoding across different data distributions, characterizes scaling of required depth and achievable compression, and highlights algorithm-specific robustness phenomena such as the apparent self-correction behavior of QFT under high-fidelity approximate inputs.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-006, C-007, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-010, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study is structured in two clear stages—training approximate amplitude encoders and then benchmarking downstream algorithms—using standard MQT Bench implementations for Grover, amplitude-estimation-based algorithms, and QFT to ensure consistency. It evaluates multiple VQC ansaetze under several synthetic input distributions (uniform noisy, periodic sparse-sine, and random normal amplitudes), examining trainability, state-fidelity metrics, and depth compression, and quantifies compression–fidelity trade-offs via factors like 2× and 5× depth reduction and fidelity thresholds around 95%.   DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Beyond its core technical findings, the paper underscores that current NISQ hardware—with high gate error rates and low coherence times—further tightens effective circuit-depth budgets, reinforcing the motivation for approximate data embeddings, and it offers a qualitative hypothesis that QFT’s robustness arises from it acting as a high-frequency noise filter analogous to classical signal processing.

VaR is similarly computed by applying QAE to a discretized loss distribution with a threshold function to extract the desired quantile. Portfolio optimization is handled through a hybrid QAOA workflow: the mean‑variance problem is converted into an Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the optimal asset subset, solved approximately by a NISQ‑suitable variational QAOA routine, followed by classical routines to infer final asset weights. The BQ-Bank platform is designed to run these quantum routines either on real superconducting hardware or via classical emulation and to reuse the option‑pricing backend for the revenues module.

In their portfolio optimization example, they impose strong simplifying assumptions: all assets are assumed to have identical price (set to 1), the investment budget must be an integer multiple of this price, and the entire budget must be fully invested. === PAPER 8f553bfb1077 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as simulating trajectories of stochastic processes—particularly Brownian motion, fractional Brownian motion, and certain Lévy processes—in a way that enables coherent quantum Monte Carlo estimation of time-averaged quantities and expectations relevant to tasks like variance swap pricing and anomalous diffusion testing. The authors argue that to gain a quantum advantage in Monte Carlo, one must be able to simulate the underlying random variable or stochastic process in quantum superposition and in an analog form where the process value at each time is stored in the amplitude of the quantum state rather than in digital registers. Fractional Brownian motion is introduced as a key target process family, and end‑to‑end applications include financial derivatives such as variance swaps and statistical tests for anomalous diffusion in time series.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-014, C-015, C-026, C-041, C-043, C-047, C-050, C-052]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum approach is a spectral (Fourier-based) method that prepares analog encodings of stochastic trajectories by first encoding suitable Fourier/Wiener coefficients and then applying a quantum Fourier or discrete sine transform to obtain process values in amplitudes. A central design choice is analog state encoding, where time-series values are compressed into amplitudes rather than stored digitally, with coherent versions of these encodings tailored for compatibility with amplitude estimation in quantum Monte Carlo. Implementation hinges on efficient, recursive data loaders based on binary-tree recursive beam splitter structures that can coherently load Gaussian amplitude distributions, including iid Gaussian vectors and Gaussian states with differing variances, and exploit permutation invariance and truncation of the Fourier series to reduce cost. For Brownian motion, the method uses a truncated Wiener-series representation; for fractional Brownian motion, it generalizes the Brownian algorithm by adjusting the power-law exponents of Fourier coefficients; for Lévy processes and stochastic integrals, it leverages the flat spectrum of Lévy white noise, Toeplitz-to-circulant embedding, and QFT-based diagonalization to produce (typically incoherent) amplitude encodings of stochastic integrals. Quantum Monte Carlo is then realized by applying standard amplitude estimation to these analog encodings, with additional circuitry to encode test functions or payoffs and, where relevant, postselection over subsets of paths.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-018, C-019, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-050]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim polylogarithmic-in-T gate complexity for simulating T time steps of fractional Brownian motion, achieved via analog spectral methods that prepare ε‑approximate analog encodings of Brownian and fractional Brownian trajectories, with formal runtime theorems for both Brownian motion and fractional Brownian motion. For Brownian motion, they prove that retaining L = O(1/ε) terms in the truncated Wiener series suffices to achieve ε‑approximate analog encodings and provide a theorem for coherent analog encodings specifically tailored to quantum Monte Carlo. For fractional Brownian motion, a corresponding theorem states that ε‑approximate analog encodings can be generated with resource bounds that lead to an end‑to‑end quantum Monte Carlo algorithm whose gate complexity scales as eO(polylog(T)/ε^{1+1/(2H)}) and which can estimate expectations of inner products or time averages over fractional Brownian paths to additive error ε. They also state correctness theorems for the Brownian simulator and for a postselected stochastic-integral algorithm that produces amplitude encodings of ∫ K(s,t) dμ_s with success probability bounded below, and they highlight specific applications including efficient pricing (under certain conditions) of variance swaps using realized variance and construction of a statistical test for anomalous diffusion using fractional Gaussian noise encodings. Additionally, they note that the power spectrum of Lévy white noise is flat, supporting the extension of their spectral method to Lévy processes, and they extend their Monte Carlo estimators to ergodicity-related metrics for Lévy processes.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-014, C-015, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-043, C-044, C-047, C-050, C-052]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper explicitly contrasts its quantum Monte Carlo algorithms with both classical and standard quantum baselines, stating that classical Monte Carlo for the target estimation problems runs in time O(T ε^{-2}) while standard quantum mean estimation achieves O(T ε^{-1}), whereas their proposed end‑to‑end algorithms can estimate certain time averages over processes in time O(polylog(T) ε^{-c}) for some c between 3/2 and 2. For stochastic-process simulation, they note that if one already has a classical sampler for the sequence of process values v_1,…,v_T with cost f(T), then a straightforward digital quantum simulation with comparable scaling exists but does not yield a speedup, in contrast to their analog encoding which compresses time into amplitudes and achieves polylogarithmic dependence on T. They further provide classical Monte Carlo and classical Fourier/spectral baselines in their discussion of variance-swap pricing and fractional Brownian Monte Carlo, emphasizing that in settings like variance swap pricing the classical problem has closed-form solutions, so any speedup should be viewed as a black‑box or oracle-model comparison rather than a white‑box complexity separation.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-007, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several important limitations. For the extension to Lévy processes, they explicitly state that their simulation guarantees are weaker than for fractional Brownian motion and that they can only provide an incoherent simulation, which prevents direct use with amplitude estimation for full quantum Monte Carlo speedups. They note that their variance-swap pricing example is constrained by the fact that this particular option has a closed-form analytical solution, so the example does not constitute a genuine white‑box speedup. They further emphasize that quantifying practical speedups requires careful comparison to potentially faster classical methods, which they leave outside the paper’s scope. In their anomalous diffusion application, they highlight that it remains an open problem to use their analog encoding for very small Hurst parameter H (deeply subdiffusive regimes), signalling a performance or applicability limitation in that parameter regime.
    [codes: C-020, C-021, C-024, C-048, C-051]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper outlines multiple directions for future research. They pose the question of whether their techniques can yield a genuine white‑box quantum speedup for financial and statistical applications, beyond the black‑box comparisons and closed‑form cases currently analyzed. They also suggest extending their approach by using mild postselection over subsets of process trajectories (for example, conditioning on path norms lying within [B_min, B_max]) as a route to tackle problems without closed-form solutions, including more complex variance-linked products. At the methodological level, they ask whether the quantum spectral method can be generalized to broader families of stochastic processes beyond the Brownian, fractional Brownian, and Lévy cases considered, and whether their techniques admit a de‑quantization, i.e., an efficient classical analogue. In the anomalous diffusion context, they explicitly leave open the challenge of effectively using their analog encodings for very small Hurst parameters, corresponding to strongly subdiffusive dynamics.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-022, C-023, C-049, C-051]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The core novelty claimed is a quantum spectral method that prepares analog encodings of stochastic-process trajectories with polylogarithmic dependence on the number of time steps, enabling end‑to‑end quantum Monte Carlo algorithms whose runtime is O(polylog(T) ε^{-c}) and thus potentially offering quantum advantage over classical Monte Carlo and standard quantum mean-estimation approaches for certain tasks. A key technical contribution they highlight is an efficient algorithm to coherently load quantum states with Gaussian amplitudes of differing variances, implemented via recursive data loader circuits whose parameters can be sampled independently and which exploit permutation invariance of iid Gaussian vectors; this Gaussian loading subroutine is presented as a standalone tool of independent interest. Conceptually, they also emphasize the importance of analog, amplitude-based representations of stochastic processes—as opposed to straightforward digital encodings—and the use of Fourier-basis representations (via QFT and related transforms) to leverage stationarity and cyclic-shift symmetries in stochastic processes, along with generalizations to Lévy processes via Toeplitz-to-circulant embedding.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-018, C-019, C-025, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-039, C-041, C-044]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is largely theoretical and algorithmic: it specifies spectral representations of Brownian and fractional Brownian motion, defines quantum primitives such as the QFT and recursive data loaders, and proves correctness and runtime theorems for analog and coherent encodings, but does not rely on empirical benchmarks or real financial datasets. The authors provide explicit constructions, such as the Brownian motion Fourier/Wiener series representation and the fractional Brownian integral definition, along with detailed descriptions of the data loader’s binary-tree structure and the distributions of its angles, which support reproducibility of the state-preparation subroutines at the level of mathematical specification. They detail how the expectation value is encoded as the success probability of measuring an ancilla qubit, how amplitude estimation links this probability to an eigenphase of an oscillating system, and how a bounded‑variance mean estimation theorem underpins their resource analysis, including specific constructions for Gaussian state preparation, payoff-function discretization, sequential path computation for Asian options, and a single‑qubit phase-estimation surrogate used in simulations.

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that applying amplitude estimation to the encoded payoff yields an (almost) quadratic reduction in the number of oracle calls compared with straightforward sampling, including a bounded‑variance version that preserves this improvement. For European and Asian options, they show that the quantum scheme approximates the corresponding Black–Scholes prices while respecting discretization and approximation errors, and they analytically bound the variance of the option to justify the applicability of their mean-estimation framework. Numerically, using a single‑qubit phase-estimation surrogate, they exhibit power‑law error scaling consistent with the theoretical quantum upper bound and find an almost quadratic advantage in estimation overhead across different strike prices, with plots comparing classical and quantum error curves and their exponents.

Critically, they assume that the martingale measure (distribution of underlying random variables) is known and that the corresponding quantum states can be prepared efficiently, and they additionally assume efficient computability of derivative payoff functions—assumptions that may be nontrivial in realistic settings.

=== PAPER 9b277c9234e8 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the computation of conditional expectations of stochastic processes via the Feynman–Kac formula, relevant for expectations of SDEs that underlie many financial models. It frames the problem as solving Feynman–Kac partial differential equations, including multi-dimensional diffusion equations, by exploiting their correspondence to a Wick‑rotated Schrödinger equation and associated generators. Rather than simulate SDE paths directly, the authors propose bypassing the SDE and instead simulating the deterministic PDE that encodes these expectations.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-015]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a hybrid variational quantum imaginary time evolution (VarQITE) algorithm tailored to the Feynman–Kac PDE: the PDE is discretized (with periodic boundary conditions) and mapped to a Hermitian Hamiltonian using Pauli/Unitary decompositions, then evolved variationally under McLachlan’s principle, with the resulting parameter ODE solved classically. The method enforces approximate l1‑normalization of a probability‑encoding quantum state via a proxy norm and simple Hadamard‑based oracles, includes an explicit algorithmic workflow (Algorithm 1), and uses a RealAmplitudes ansatz with real‑valued amplitudes and classically optimized initialization. The construction relies on decomposing the differential operator into unitaries and ensuring constant diffusion coefficients so that the effective Hamiltonian is Hermitian, while tracking both l1 and l2 norms during evolution.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On a two‑dimensional anisotropic heat/Feynman–Kac example implemented with 6‑ and 8‑qubit RealAmplitudes ansätze, the authors report remarkable agreement between the variational quantum method and classical solvers, supported by comparisons to an exact heat‑kernel solution. They observe that increasing the number of ansatz layers improves the match between VarQITE and forward Euler, reducing previously visible discrepancies in the evolution curves. Across the simulated cases, the l1 norm is kept approximately normalized by the proxy mechanism, and the l2‑norm differences versus classical baselines remain modest for the illustrative low‑qubit settings.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-040]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The variational quantum algorithm is benchmarked against classical ODE/PDE solvers (including forward Euler) and Monte Carlo simulation on a (2+1)‑dimensional Feynman–Kac system, with an exact heat‑kernel solution available as a further reference. The authors report that, for their test instances, the quantum and classical methods agree remarkably well, and that as more layers are added to the ansatz the plots of VarQITE and forward Euler align more closely and eliminate earlier discrepancies. Complexity‑wise, they contrast their readout strategy—aiming for quadratic speedup in extracting moments—with classical Monte Carlo scaling as O(T/ε²), while also analyzing algorithmic costs such as the O(N³) scaling of the linear systems solved in each variational update.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-006, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-027, C-032, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly warns that potential quantum advantages may be significantly reduced by practical issues in the readout stage, notably the difficulty of constructing the required oracle Sf and the amplification of estimation error by the normalization factor ∥f∥₂. The proposed l1‑normalization enforcement via a proxy norm is only approximate and its accuracy is limited, which can impact solution fidelity. From an algorithmic perspective, the expressivity‑barren plateau tradeoff constrains ansatz design, and the authors note that in high‑dimensional cases the chosen VarQITE ansatz will limit attainable accuracy. They also report numerical instabilities arising from required numerical differentiation when increasing layers and qubits, and acknowledge that finite‑sampling and hardware noise are not included in their simulations, so the reported performance does not reflect full NISQ‑era noise. Overall, they emphasize that readout caveats, normalization issues, ansatz limitations, and numerical instability can all diminish or negate the theoretical speedups.
    [codes: C-024, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-041]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors point to several future application directions, especially in quantitative finance, including extending their Feynman–Kac‑based framework to stochastic volatility and stochastic interest rate models, and to American and other decision‑embedded options. They also suggest applying the algorithm beyond the heat equation to other PDEs such as Poisson and wave equations, and indicate that Appendix H outlines additional exploratory items and prospective finance applications.
    [codes: C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as a unified algorithmic framework that leverages variational quantum imaginary time evolution to solve Feynman–Kac PDEs—thus computing expectations of SDEs on quantum hardware by mapping them to Wick‑rotated Schrödinger‑type equations. This includes the strategic bypass of direct SDE simulation in favor of deterministic PDE evolution, and the introduction of a proxy norm mechanism for approximately preserving probability normalization during non‑ℓ₂‑preserving imaginary‑time‑like dynamics. The authors summarize these ideas in an explicit algorithm (Algorithm 1) intended as a general method for Feynman–Kac‑type problems.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-030]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper builds on a rigorous stochastic‑calculus foundation (e.g., existence of Brownian motion and formal derivation of Feynman–Kac in one and multiple dimensions) before discretization and quantum mapping. It carefully documents discretization choices such as periodic boundary conditions and the construction of the infinitesimal generator, and derives the variational dynamics using McLachlan’s principle with an explicit O(N³) cost for solving the associated linear systems. The numerical section explains the concrete anisotropic heat‑equation test case, ansatz selection (RealAmplitudes with real amplitudes), and classical initialization of parameters, and it tracks both ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ norms during evolution. The authors also discuss readout design and complexity, emphasizing that often only properties (e.g., moments) of the solution are read out, and that classical Monte Carlo scaling provides the baseline they aim to improve upon.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None beyond the above; all verified codes fit within the main analytical dimensions.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames Quantum Monte Carlo Integration (QMCI) as a way to accelerate high-dimensional Monte Carlo expectations arising in finance, particularly for path-dependent derivatives and portfolio risk measures. It formulates expectations as quantum amplitudes via affine transformations and Born-rule measurement, targeting applications such as look-back and other path-dependent options where Monte Carlo is ubiquitous in mathematical finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-013, C-014, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-041]

They avoid deep quantum arithmetic by decomposing integrands into Fourier series so each harmonic uses a shallow circuit, leverage reversible classical sampling circuits and parameterized loaders to prepare distributions such as Gaussians/Brownian motion, and implement an enhanced P-builder providing arithmetic, logic, indicator qubits, and max/sum constructions tailored to financial payoffs. The engine also contains a resource mode with NISQ and fault-tolerant sub-modes, and includes noise-aware QAE and fault-tolerant synthesis error bounds for realistic circuit assessment.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that, after appropriate rescaling, QMCI estimators retain quadratic RMSE scaling in the number of QAE queries, parameterized via a constant c_QAE that depends on the specific QAE variant. LCU QAE is empirically benchmarked to have significantly better statistical robustness than MLQAE and IQAE under the authors’ metrics, while maintaining comparable convergence speed. For distribution loading, Gaussian and lognormal parametrized quantum circuit loaders achieve very small fitting errors, leading the authors to judge them suitable for simple financial calculations, and they construct Fourier-series estimators for mean, variance/second moment, and (conditional) exponential expectations, showing that conditional exponentials inherit the exponential convergence properties of the unconditional exponential case. They tabulate classical–quantum convergence and crossover thresholds and provide detailed NISQ and fault-tolerant resource counts for path-dependent option benchmarks, including barrier, look-back, and autocallable products.
    [codes: C-015, C-019, C-025, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-041, C-044]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors contrast QMCI’s RMSE scaling—proportional to the reciprocal of the number of samples under QAE—with classical Monte Carlo’s 1/√q behavior, and formalize this via a generic convergence expression with a QAE-dependent constant. They compile tables comparing classical and quantum Monte Carlo convergences, including the number of samples required to reach given RMSE thresholds, and present classical–quantum crossover points where the quadratic advantage would theoretically appear for their benchmark instruments.
    [codes: C-005, C-019, C-035]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that many standard QAE estimators are not statistically robust, exhibiting skewed and heavy-tailed error distributions, which motivates the introduction of LCU QAE rather than claiming existing methods as ready for deployment. It critiques Grover–Rudolph state preparation as a false economy because it relies on classical Monte Carlo, and notes that its own exponential-expectation benchmarks focus on a low-volatility setting (σ = 0.1) as a practical restriction. The authors emphasize that NISQ execution is foreseeable only for smaller, four-time-slice benchmarks, implying that larger, more realistic path-dependent problems remain beyond current devices. They also state that their fault-tolerant resource bounds are conservative and can be tightened by assuming more realistic, iid approximation errors, and they stress that moving from theoretical to useful quantum advantage depends on many external factors beyond asymptotic scaling.
    [codes: C-010, C-016, C-033, C-040, C-045, C-047]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors expect that as hardware scales, the QMCI engine will deliver utility before full quantum advantage is achieved, and they point to Greeks computation and portfolio risk/optimisation as principal future beneficiaries once larger problem sizes become tractable. They argue that further progress toward useful quantum advantage will require addressing a host of external factors, not just improving asymptotic performance, implying additional work on hardware, algorithms, and integration into financial workflows.
    [codes: C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s main contribution is a modular, extensible QMCI engine specifically architected for financial applications, including an enhanced P-builder for constructing complex derivative payoffs and portfolio-risk circuits, a Fourier-based QMCI scheme that avoids deep quantum arithmetic while retaining quadratic advantage, and a new LCU QAE variant designed for statistically robust amplitude estimation with a fail-fast property. Additionally, the authors highlight a dual-mode resource module (NISQ and fault-tolerant) that quantifies resources for both current small-scale demonstrations and future large-scale QMCI tasks.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-018, C-026, C-027, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work defines explicit statistical robustness metrics (bias, variance-related measures, skewness, kurtosis) for evaluating QAE variants and conducts dedicated robustness benchmarks for LCU QAE against MLQAE and IQAE. The enhanced P-builder and Fourier constructions are illustrated with concrete examples like look-back options and Brownian motion built from summed Gaussians, and the benchmark suite uses standardized path-dependent instruments and discrete Gaussian time-series models to reflect common mathematical-finance Monte Carlo tasks. The resource mode distinguishes clearly between NISQ and fault-tolerant settings and introduces an explicit approximation-error model for synthesis, later discussing how its conservativeness might be reduced, indicating attention to rigor in resource estimation.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes that noise-aware QAE can treat inclement noise as an effective Gaussian random variable regardless of detailed underlying characteristics, which is incorporated as background technique within the engine but not tied to a single experiment. === PAPER 9ecabb9df454 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses computational bottlenecks in financial risk measurement for large portfolios, where VaR, CVaR, higher-moment and systemic risk metrics are expensive to compute under complex correlation structures and dynamic market conditions. It reformulates portfolio risk and covariance structures as quantum observables and entangled states, posing risk computation and portfolio optimization as problems over quantum-encoded portfolios and risk Hamiltonians. The work is motivated by the limitations of classical Monte Carlo–based risk assessment and the lack of comprehensive theoretical foundations for quantum risk modeling.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-027, C-044]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a family of quantum methods: (i) encoding portfolios and their covariance matrices into quantum states with entanglement capturing asset correlations, and defining variance, VaR, CVaR and higher risk measures as quantum observables; (ii) using quantum amplitude estimation to compute VaR and CVaR with quadratic speedup; and (iii) formulating portfolio optimization as finding the ground state of a risk Hamiltonian and applying counterdiabatic quantum annealing (including approximate counterdiabatic evolution) to accelerate convergence. They also introduce methods for dynamic risk assessment with time-dependent covariance matrices, structural decompositions (e.g., block-diagonal sectors), and hybrid quantum–classical decomposition strategies for practical implementations.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-021, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-038, C-039, C-044, C-048]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports theoretical results including exponentially compact representations of high-dimensional portfolios and covariance structures, qualitative links between correlation strength and entanglement, and accuracy bounds plus convergence theorems for quantum algorithms computing VaR, CVaR and higher-moment risk measures. It establishes complexity expressions for quantum risk computation, showing quadratic speedups for VaR and CVaR via amplitude estimation and characterizing conditions (e.g., portfolio size, sparsity, and covariance conditioning) under which polynomial to exponential speedups over classical Monte Carlo can emerge. For portfolio optimization, the authors prove that counterdiabatic annealing can reduce annealing time, guarantee convergence to the ground-state (optimal) portfolio under uniqueness assumptions, and achieve (1+ε)-approximate solutions with specified overhead. They further show that in dynamic settings quantum risk algorithms adapt to time-varying covariance matrices with polynomial overhead and bounded incremental update costs, while also deriving theoretical bounds on noise tolerance and on fundamental limits to quantum speedup. Overall, they summarize these as comprehensive theoretical foundations with provable performance guarantees and practical design principles.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-022, C-024, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly compare their quantum methods against classical Monte Carlo–based risk computation, noting that classical approaches for VaR, CVaR and related metrics require O(1/ε²) samples to achieve precision ε. They derive classical versus quantum complexity expressions and argue that quantum algorithms, particularly those based on amplitude estimation, can reduce this dependence to achieve quadratic speedups in precision and, for well-structured or sparse covariance matrices and sufficiently large portfolios, polynomial to exponential speedups in overall complexity relative to classical baselines.
    [codes: C-015, C-026, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-057]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several theoretical and practical limitations. It proves that for portfolios with arbitrary, unstructured correlation matrices, quantum algorithms cannot achieve exponential speedup in the worst case because of input/output bottlenecks, thereby setting fundamental limits on speedups. It also derives a maximum tolerable gate error rate for the proposed quantum risk algorithms, indicating that noise levels above this threshold would compromise performance guarantees. More broadly, the authors frame their results as contingent on structural properties such as favorable conditioning or sparsity of the covariance matrix, implying that in ill-structured or highly noisy regimes the advantages may be limited.
    [codes: C-036, C-037, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors outline an agenda of open problems, including tightening complexity bounds for quantum risk computation, developing algorithms for non-Gaussian and fat-tailed return distributions, and extending the framework to multi-period portfolio optimization with transaction costs. They also call for quantum methods tailored to high-frequency trading risk assessment and for investigations into quantum machine learning approaches for predictive risk modeling.
    [codes: C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to establish comprehensive theoretical foundations for quantum-enhanced financial risk modeling, including rigorous mathematical frameworks for representing risk as quantum observables with entangled covariance encoding, complexity analyses, convergence theorems, and design principles tailored to financial applications. It emphasizes providing provable performance guarantees, identifying structural conditions for quantum advantage, extending the theory to dynamic risk assessment, and offering practical guidelines and pathways for realizing quantum advantage in real-world risk management.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The work is purely theoretical and does not report empirical experiments or datasets; instead it presents mathematical constructions, complexity analyses, and convergence proofs for proposed quantum risk algorithms. Methodological rigor is reflected in explicit derivation of bounds, conditions for convergence and quantum advantage, and tolerance to noise, but there is no discussion of implementation details, hardware experiments, or reproducible code and data, consistent with its positioning as a foundational theoretical framework.

=== PAPER 9ee4aaf0f745 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets high-dimensional Monte Carlo-type problems in quantitative finance, specifically multi-option portfolio pricing and credit valuation adjustment (CVA), and formulates them as expectation/sampling estimation tasks amenable to quantum speedup. It shows that CVA can be recast as a variant of the multi-option pricing problem and provides formal problem statements for portfolios of independently priced derivatives and CVA expressed as discounted positive exposure weighted by default probabilities under discrete event/time grids and quantum access models. The work is motivated by the central role of Monte Carlo in such risk calculations and the practical importance of accurate CVA modelling given past market losses.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-007, C-015, C-017, C-019, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is built around quantum Monte Carlo techniques using quantum amplitude estimation (QAE), specifically the unbiased QAE algorithm of Cornelissen and Hamoudi (2023), as a core primitive to accelerate statistical sampling for expectations relevant to pricing and CVA. The algorithms assume quantum matrix and sampling access oracles for probability and payoff/exposure arrays, use general subroutines such as powering/median boosting for success amplification and quantum minimum finding for preprocessing/normalization, and rely on norm and inner-product estimation routines tailored to various access models and variance conditions. Unbiasedness of the estimator is a recurring conceptual theme underpinning the method design.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-010, C-011, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors derive quantum query-complexity bounds for approximating multi-option portfolio prices and CVA under several error regimes. For CVA without additional moment information, they provide a theorem giving access to the maximum weighted positive exposure and an estimate of E[CVA]; under bounded variance they show that an additive-error estimate of CVA can be obtained with query complexity scaling as Õ(σ(1−R)/ε log(1/δ)) and, assuming Var(CVA) ≤ B·E[CVA]^2, a relative-error estimate with Õ(B/ε log(1/δ)) queries. They also prove corresponding theorems for multi-asset portfolio pricing and, in a Black–Scholes–Merton setting for a European call, bound Var(CVA) by T^2(1−R)^2 λ̃^2 to justify the variance assumptions, leading to additive and relative error CVA guarantees (Theorems 5 and 6) with explicit error bounds in terms of ε, (1−R), and σ.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper explicitly contrasts its quantum algorithms with classical Monte Carlo baselines. It recalls that classical Monte Carlo sample complexity scales as O(σ^2/ε^2) for additive error, and for CVA with additive error ε obtains a classical complexity of O(σ^2(1−R)^2/ε^2 log(1/δ)). For multi-option portfolios, the authors cite the use of ℓ1-sampling techniques (Tang, 2019) to characterize the classical query complexity. On this basis, they state that their quantum methods, leveraging QAE-based Monte Carlo, suggest a quadratic speedup in query complexity over the corresponding classical schemes for both portfolio pricing and CVA in the regimes considered.
    [codes: C-012, C-035, C-036, C-034]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The analysis is carried out under several structural and statistical assumptions that limit generality. The main problem formulation focuses on portfolios of K derivatives that can be priced independently in finite settings, restricting attention to independent, finite event spaces and discrete time grids. The quantum algorithms assume specific forms of quantum access to probability and payoff/exposure matrices, including knowledge of the ℓ1-norm of the probability vector, which the authors argue is reasonable but nonetheless is an input requirement. Several key subroutines and improved estimators require bounded-norm or bounded-variance conditions (e.g., ‖w‖1 bounded by a constant, ‖w‖1 ≤ σ^2, and a relative variance bound ‖w‖1‖z‖2^2 ≤ B), and the enhanced CVA bounds rely on the existence of explicit variance bounds, such as those derived in a Black–Scholes–Merton European call setting. The paper also notes that prior CVA quantisation work used numerous heuristics and depth-reduction techniques for near-term devices, whereas their results are positioned in a more idealized, fault-tolerant setting, highlighting that practical resource and implementation constraints on current hardware are not resolved here.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-019, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-031, C-013]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose several extensions: adapting their theoretically grounded algorithms with heuristics and circuit-depth reduction techniques to assess performance on near-term quantum devices, extending the quantum treatment of credit risk to bilateral credit risk settings, and studying potential quantum speedups for other XVA components such as Margin Valuation Adjustment (MVA).
    [codes: C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as providing quantum algorithms that provably accelerate Monte Carlo-style sampling for multi-option portfolio pricing and CVA, including a theoretical quantum speedup in a fault-tolerant setting where such speedups for CVA had not been previously established. The work unifies CVA and multi-option pricing as related sampling problems, systematically reworks and enhances earlier quantum Monte Carlo algorithms using the unbiased QAE of Cornelissen and Hamoudi (2023) across several settings, and improves on prior heuristic CVA quantisation by deriving rigorous query-complexity bounds, particularly under bounded-variance assumptions that allow stronger approximation guarantees than earlier general approaches.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-014, C-032, C-033, C-013, C-034]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The paper is analytical and method-development focused, with rigour grounded in formal theorems and lemmas rather than empirical experiments or datasets. It carefully documents general quantum subroutines (e.g., unbiased amplitude estimation with variance bounds, norm and inner-product estimation under different access models) that underpin reproducibility of the complexity analysis. Assumptions such as known probability-vector norms and bounded variance are explicitly stated and, in the CVA context, justified through model-based derivations in the Black–Scholes–Merton setting, while classical baselines are derived or cited to enable clear theoretical comparisons. However, there is no indication of numerical simulations, hardware experiments, or benchmark datasets being used or evaluated.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-012, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper discusses the broader quantitative finance context motivating XVA and CVA, including questioning how far valuation should deviate from the Black–Scholes–Merton paradigm based on counterparty-specific characteristics, and noting that failures in modelling such risks have led to large financial losses. It also highlights that quantum amplitude estimation has emerged as a particularly useful primitive in quantum algorithms, with unbiasedness becoming a prevalent conceptual focus.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames insurance and actuarial work as fundamentally about modeling and evaluating random risky events, and notes that growing data size and model complexity in insurance create computational challenges that motivate new approaches. Within this context, it systematically organizes insurance problems into stochastic modeling, optimization, and machine-learning-based tasks, covering non-life (e.g., policy excess, IBNR), life (e.g., contract valuation, Lee–Carter mortality forecasting, multi-period optimization), and risk management tasks (e.g., VaR, cVaR, reinsurance allocation).

  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a general quantum framework where probability distributions are encoded via quantum state preparation, risk processes are analyzed with quantum stochastic simulation, collective risks are addressed with quantum optimization, and data-driven models use quantum machine learning, distinguishing NISQ-era variational methods from fault-tolerant linear-algebra-based approaches. Concretely, they discuss quantum stochastic modeling with amplitude encoding and quantum Monte Carlo, QUBO-to-Ising mappings for optimization solvable via quantum annealing and QAOA-like methods, and implement specific algorithms: a discrete quantum excess evaluation circuit using n+2 qubits, a reinsurance variance-minimization Hamiltonian optimized with a constraint-preserving ansatz and measurement-based error mitigation, and a Lee–Carter mortality solver based on quantum singular value decomposition on 4 qubits with real mortality data.

In numerical simulations of the quantum excess evaluation algorithm, the estimated excess payment converges toward the truncated reference value as the number of qubits increases. On real hardware, the reinsurance allocation experiment shows the loss function decreasing during variational optimization, and the Lee–Carter QSVD experiment similarly reports decreasing loss and improved fit over optimization steps. The authors further assert that solving the Lee–Carter mortality forecasting model on a quantum processor with real mortality data constitutes the first implementation of an insurance-specific quantum algorithm on a quantum processor using real datasets and, more broadly, the first time an insurance-specific real-world data problem is experimentally solved on real quantum computers.
    [codes: C-023, C-028, C-033, C-036, C-010, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors conceptually compare their quantum stochastic modeling approach to classical Monte Carlo, asserting that amplitude encoding combined with quantum Monte Carlo can provide exponential savings in state space and a quadratic speedup over classical sampling-based methods.     [codes: C-023, C-026, C-028]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that in the NISQ era, both the number of available qubits and the allowable circuit depth are limited by noise, constraining the scale of feasible insurance computations on current hardware. It also explicitly notes that preparing quantum states corresponding to general probability distributions may require exponential resources, highlighting state preparation as a major bottleneck. Additionally, the authors point out that single-shot readout, where each shot yields only one n-bit string, greatly limits efficiency in extracting information from quantum states.
    [codes: C-038, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors outline a staged timetable for quantum computational insurance, distinguishing what may be achievable in the NISQ era versus fault-tolerant quantum computing, and express the belief that both theoretical and experimental breakthroughs in quantum insurance and actuarial science will be achieved.     [codes: C-009, C-039, C-042]

Specifically, they highlight solving the Lee–Carter mortality forecasting model as the first implementation of an insurance-specific quantum algorithm on a quantum processor with real data, and more broadly as the first time an insurance-specific real-world data problem has been experimentally solved on actual quantum hardware.

They categorize insurance tasks into stochastic modeling, optimization, and machine-learning-based problems and map each to corresponding quantum primitives such as state preparation, stochastic simulation, optimization, and quantum machine learning. In their hardware experiments, they use a problem-specific, constraint-preserving ansatz for the reinsurance allocation task and apply measurement-based error mitigation to counter noise, while the Lee–Carter experiment uses real-world mortality data structured into a small (4×4) matrix to keep the problem tractable on current devices. === PAPER a0bb411d1801 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as modeling financial asset price evolution and return distributions using discrete-time quantum walks instead of standard stochastic processes. It is motivated by specific shortcomings of classical models, such as the inability of geometric Brownian motion to capture asymmetric returns, fat tails, and temporal dependence in returns, and by the lack of a one-size-fits-all model for market behavior. The proposed approach aims to generate richer, potentially asymmetric and extreme-event-prone return distributions and to provide temporal asset price dynamics via the quantum walk’s evolution.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The method is a one-dimensional discrete-time quantum walk with a two-dimensional coin, formulated on a tensor-product Hilbert space where each time step consists of a coin operation followed by a conditional shift, and measurement yields position probabilities interpreted as returns. The dynamics are governed by a reduced set of coin parameters (η and θ), with randomness arising from quantum measurement rather than stochastic transitions, and the usual Wiener process in a stochastic differential equation is conceptually replaced by a quantum-walk process, with an auxiliary scaling function f(t) proposed to compensate for ballistic diffusion. The authors also discuss efficient implementation of a quantum-walk circuit on gate-based quantum hardware and extend the model to include decoherence (e.g., link breaking) to interpolate between quantum and classical behavior.
    [codes: C-007, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Analytically and via simulations, the authors find that the unitary quantum walk exhibits ballistic diffusion, with variance growing quadratically in the number of time steps and distribution width increasing with time, but this can be normalized by rescaling positions. They show that initial coin states and coin parameters can bias the distribution toward increasing or decreasing prices and can be interpreted as modeling bubbles, corrections, and other asymmetric market tendencies; skewness, variance, and Shannon entropy are used to quantify asymmetry, unpredictability, and uncertainty, with variance strongly dependent on θ and entropy maximized for the Hadamard coin. Introducing decoherence (e.g., via broken links) produces a quantum-to-classical transition, and for intermediate decoherence strengths the distributions are non-Gaussian with fat tails and higher probabilities of extreme events than classical models, while entropy rises with decoherence and can approach a maximum, leading the authors to claim that quantum-walk models offer flexible return shapes (including bimodal and extreme-event behavior) with well-behaved higher moments and the ability to generate return distributions via time evolution.
    [codes: C-021, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper explicitly compares return distributions generated by the quantum-walk model to those from classical methodologies such as geometric Brownian motion, Lévy-stable/power-law models, and classical random walks. The authors stress that GBM yields symmetric, Gaussian-tailed returns with independent increments and thus misses frequent large price changes, while Lévy-stable models can match heavy tails but suffer from divergent variance for α < 2, and they argue that different markets require different modeling approaches. In contrast, they claim the quantum walk (especially with decoherence) can overcome these limitations by producing fatter-than-Gaussian tails without divergent higher moments and by offering greater flexibility in shape (e.g., biases, bimodality, and decoherence effects) while recovering classical behavior in the strong-decoherence limit, including having return distributions with fatter tails than Gaussian in their illustrative comparison.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors note several limitations of prevailing classical models that motivate their work, including GBM’s symmetric returns, thin Gaussian tails, and lack of temporal correlations, as well as Lévy-stable models’ divergent variance for certain tail exponents. At the same time, they acknowledge that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to modeling return distributions and emphasize that different markets may require different models, implicitly limiting the universality of their own proposal. A key self-acknowledged limitation of the study is that it is purely theoretical and uses no historical financial data, so the quantum-walk model is not empirically validated here, which the authors explicitly flag in the data availability statement.

In particular, the authors highlight as contributions the ability of the quantum-walk model to generate asymmetric, fat-tailed, and dynamically evolving return distributions (including bubble- and correction-like behaviors), to incorporate decoherence as a tunable bridge between quantum and classical regimes, and to avoid divergent higher moments while producing distributions through intrinsic time evolution rather than imposed parametric forms.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study is entirely based on synthetic data generated by analytic/simulation analysis of the quantum-walk formalism, with no empirical financial datasets used. They also perform smoothing of spiky quantum-walk distributions via histogram aggregation to better approximate realistic financial data, and interpret entropy changes as potential indicators of turbulent market regimes, but reproducibility is limited by the lack of shared code and by the absence of real-data calibration or validation.
